paper_heading: Maynez et al. (2020)
summary_text: Joshua Maynez, Shashi Narayan, Bernd Bohnet, and Ryan McDonald. “On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization.” *Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics*, 1906–1919, 2020. DOI: [10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.173](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2020.acl-main.173); [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.173/). Maynez et al. conduct a large-scale human evaluation of abstractive summarization systems and analyze the kinds of content that is not supported by the input document. They find substantial hallucinated content across generated summaries, while pretrained systems perform better than earlier systems on both automatic metrics and human judgments of faithfulness and factuality; textual-entailment measures correlate with human faithfulness judgments better than standard overlap metrics such as ROUGE. The study is limited by its focus on document summarization and by the difficulty of reducing human judgments of factuality and faithfulness to a single general criterion. For this project, its key contribution is the distinction between source-grounded faithfulness and broader factuality, which supports labeling claims as entailed by supplied premises, contradicted by them, or unsupported rather than treating every factual error as the same phenomenon.

paper_heading: Ji et al. (2023)
summary_text: Ziwei Ji, Nayeon Lee, Rita Frieske, Tiezheng Yu, Dan Su, Yan Xu, Etsuko Ishii, Yejin Bang, Delong Chen, Wenliang Dai, Ho Shu Chan, Andrea Madotto, and Pascale Fung. “Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation.” *ACM Computing Surveys* 55(12), 1–38, 2023. DOI: [10.1145/3571730](https://doi.org/10.1145/3571730); [arXiv:2202.03629](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03629). This survey synthesizes definitions, evaluation metrics, mitigation methods, and task-specific findings across abstractive summarization, dialogue, generative question answering, data-to-text generation, machine translation, visual-language generation, and large language models. Its central organizing distinction is intrinsic hallucination, where an output contradicts the source, versus extrinsic hallucination, where an output is neither supported nor contradicted by the source. The breadth of the review is also its limitation: it inventories heterogeneous tasks and methods, but does not provide a single reasoning representation that explains how claims, premises, warrants, and conclusions relate across those tasks. It is directly relevant as a seed taxonomy for span-level labeling and as evidence that detection must be conditioned on the source and task; this project extends that foundation with an explicit argument structure and auditable provenance.

paper_heading: Rawte et al. (2023)
summary_text: Vipula Rawte, Swagata Chakraborty, Agnibh Pathak, Anubhav Sarkar, S. M. Towhidul Islam Tonmoy, Aman Chadha, Amit Sheth, and Amitava Das. “The Troubling Emergence of Hallucination in Large Language Models — An Extensive Definition, Quantification, and Prescriptive Remediations.” *Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing*, 2541–2573, 2023. DOI: [10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.155](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2023.emnlp-main.155); [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.155/). Rawte et al. propose a fine-grained framework that profiles hallucination by orientation, degree, and category, distinguishing “factual mirage” from “silver lining,” subdividing each by intrinsic and extrinsic status and by severity, and introducing six named error types; they also release the 75,000-sample HILT dataset and propose a Hallucination Vulnerability Index for comparing models. The paper’s strength is its insistence that hallucination is a family of mismatches requiring differentiated measurement and remediation rather than one binary defect. Its limitation for this project is that broad orientation, severity, and category labels do not by themselves identify which premise, warrant, or conclusion failed, and the proposed index compresses heterogeneous behaviors into aggregate vulnerability. The project can therefore use Rawte et al. as a taxonomy-first precedent while making each label mechanically inspectable through span-level evidence, inferential relation, and verification status.

paper_heading: Huang et al. (2023 arXiv; 2025 ACM publication)
summary_text: Lei Huang, Weijiang Yu, Weitao Ma, Weihong Zhong, Zhangyin Feng, Haotian Wang, Qianglong Chen, Weihua Peng, Xiaocheng Feng, Bing Qin, and Ting Liu. “A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models: Principles, Taxonomy, Challenges, and Open Questions.” arXiv:2311.05232, 2023; subsequently published in *ACM Transactions on Information Systems* with DOI [10.1145/3703155](https://doi.org/10.1145/3703155); [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.05232). Huang et al. develop an LLM-specific taxonomy and review causes, detection methods, benchmarks, mitigation strategies, and open problems, including the limits of retrieval-augmented generation and the role of knowledge boundaries, long-tail knowledge, and changing world knowledge. The survey’s method is a structured synthesis of the rapidly expanding LLM hallucination literature, and its main finding is that plausible nonfactual generation persists even when models are augmented with retrieval, because retrieval quality, interpretation, and generation can each introduce unsupported content. Its limitation is that the organization is primarily by causes, methods, and benchmarks rather than by an explicit representation of the reasoning structure of individual claims. For this project, it is the closest general survey: its treatment of support, knowledge boundaries, and RAG failure motivates representing premise availability and claim status as entailed, contradicted, supported only by external evidence, or unresolved before generation.

paper_heading: Tonmoy et al. (2024)
summary_text: S. M. Towhidul Islam Tonmoy, S. M. Mehedi Zaman, Vinija Jain, Anku Rani, Vipula Rawte, Aman Chadha, and Amitava Das. “A Comprehensive Survey of Hallucination Mitigation Techniques in Large Language Models.” arXiv:2401.01313, 2024. [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01313). Tonmoy et al. survey more than 32 techniques for reducing hallucination in LLMs and classify them across dimensions including dataset use, task, feedback mechanism, and retriever type; the review covers interventions such as retrieval augmentation, knowledge retrieval, contrastive or feedback-based methods, and verification-oriented approaches. Its main contribution is a vocabulary for locating mitigation in the pipeline—before generation through grounding and retrieval, during generation through decoding or control, or after generation through checking and correction—and a discussion of the limitations that remain across these strategies. Because it is a mitigation survey, it does not supply a detailed account of the argument content that each intervention is intended to protect, and its technique-centered categories can obscure whether a method addresses a faulty premise, an invalid inference, or an unsupported conclusion. The project uses this work to evaluate compact context construction as a pre-generation grounding intervention while adding a deductive skeleton and span-level provenance so mitigation effects can be tied to specific reasoning units.

paper_heading: Venkit et al. (2024)
summary_text: Pranav Narayanan Venkit, Tatiana Chakravorti, Vipul Gupta, Heidi Biggs, Mukund Srinath, Koustava Goswami, Sarah Rajtmajer, and Shomir Wilson. “An Audit on the Perspectives and Challenges of Hallucinations in NLP.” *Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing*, 6528–6548, 2024. DOI: [10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.375](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.375); [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.375/). Venkit et al. audit how hallucination is characterized in 103 peer-reviewed NLP publications and complement that literature analysis with a survey of 171 NLP and AI practitioners. They find substantial disagreement over the meaning and scope of “hallucination,” and argue that inconsistent definitions create downstream problems for evaluation, communication, and responsible deployment; they therefore call for explicit definitions and frameworks. The audit’s limitation is that it diagnoses field-level conceptual instability rather than delivering a compact, operational grammar for classifying the relation between a claim and its evidence. Its relevance to this project is foundational: it justifies establishing an explicit ontology and schema before classification, recording the textual evidence and argument relation behind every decision so labels remain auditable across traditions and evaluators.

paper_heading: Sahoo et al. (2024)
summary_text: Pranab Sahoo, Prabhash Meharia, Akash Ghosh, Sriparna Saha, Vinija Jain, and Aman Chadha. “A Comprehensive Survey of Hallucination in Large Language, Image, Video and Audio Foundation Models.” *Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024*, 11709–11724, 2024. DOI: [10.18653/v1/2024.findings-emnlp.685](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.findings-emnlp.685); [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-emnlp.685/). Sahoo et al. broaden hallucination research beyond text by surveying definitions, taxonomies, detection methods, and mitigation across language, image, video, and audio foundation models. The paper’s central finding is that hallucination is a cross-modal reliability problem with modality-specific symptoms but recurring grounding and evidence-alignment concerns, and it proposes a framework for organizing detection and mitigation across those modalities. Its breadth necessarily leaves less room for fine-grained analysis of textual inference, and modality-specific benchmarks and metrics are not interchangeable without additional normalization. Although this project is text-centered, the survey supports a modality-neutral abstraction in which a generated claim is checked against an evidence channel and an intended task relation; the project specializes that abstraction by recovering language-level spans, premises, and conclusions for compact, high-signal context.

paper_heading: van Deemter (2024)
summary_text: Kees van Deemter. “The Pitfalls of Defining Hallucination.” *Computational Linguistics* 50(2), 807–816, 2024. DOI: [10.1162/coli_a_00509](https://doi.org/10.1162/coli_a_00509); [MIT Press](https://direct.mit.edu/coli/article/50/2/807/119144/The-Pitfalls-of-Defining-Hallucination); [arXiv:2401.07897](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.07897). van Deemter compares existing analyses of hallucination, omission, and other factual errors in data-to-text generation and proposes a logic-based synthesis using the two directions of logical consequence between input and output: whether the input entails the output and whether the output entails the input, with additional distinctions for contradiction and cases where neither side follows from the other. He shows that common taxonomies can conflate materially different errors—for example, unsupported additions, omissions, and contradictions—and argues that ambiguity, vagueness, pragmatics, and open-ended LLM tasks limit any purely logical account. The paper is limited as an operational system because it does not provide a scalable cross-tradition span extractor or context compressor, and natural-language entailment is itself difficult for ambiguous or underspecified text. It is nevertheless the most direct theoretical bridge to this project: its entailment structure supplies a principled backbone for classifying additions, omissions, contradictions, and logical independence while the project contributes the extraction, evidence, and compact-representation layers.

paper_heading: Xu, Jain, and Kankanhalli (2024)
summary_text: Ziwei Xu, Sanjay Jain, and Mohan Kankanhalli. “Hallucination Is Inevitable: An Innate Limitation of Large Language Models.” arXiv:2401.11817, 2024. [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.11817). Xu, Jain, and Kankanhalli formalize hallucination as inconsistency between a computable LLM and a computable ground-truth function, use learning-theoretic results to argue that no LLM can learn all computable functions, and conclude that hallucination cannot be eliminated for general problem solving; they further characterize hallucination-prone tasks under time-complexity constraints, validate aspects of the analysis empirically, and discuss what existing mitigations can and cannot achieve. The formal result is intentionally high-level and depends on an idealized world and assumptions about computability, so it does not constitute a complete empirical taxonomy of the diverse errors observed in deployed systems. Its relevance is the design implication that reliability systems must represent uncertainty and abstention rather than force every generated span into a binary true/false or supported/contradicted class. This project operationalizes that implication as an explicit unknown or insufficient-support status attached to a compact evidence record and reasoning skeleton.

paper_heading: Xu et al. (2023), “Are Large Language Models Really Good Logical Reasoners? A Comprehensive Evaluation and Beyond”
summary_text: Xu et al. evaluate seven LLMs across 15 datasets covering deductive, inductive, abductive, and mixed-form reasoning. Rather than treating answer accuracy as sufficient, they assess answers and explanations, classify logical flaws in evidence selection and reasoning, and propose a six-dimensional evaluation scheme that includes correctness, rigor, self-awareness, activity, orientation, and “no hallucination.” The study’s central contribution is therefore methodological: it makes unsupported or flawed reasoning an explicit evaluation dimension alongside final-answer correctness. Its limitation for this project is that the abstract-level benchmark description does not establish a reusable proof-span representation, a dedicated hallucination mechanism model, or coverage of the project’s cross-tradition argument forms. It nevertheless provides a strong precedent for scoring intermediate explanations and unsupported claims separately from final labels, supporting a deductive skeleton in which each generated edge can be checked rather than relying on answer accuracy alone. [Xu et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.09841)

paper_heading: Yuan et al. (2024), “Whispers that Shake Foundations: Analyzing and Mitigating False Premise Hallucinations in Large Language Models”
summary_text: Yuan et al. directly study false-premise hallucination, defined as generating hallucinated text when confronted with a false-premise question. Their analysis identifies a small subset of attention heads—“false premise heads”—that disrupt knowledge extraction, and they introduce FAITH, an inference-time method that constrains those heads. The paper reports that constraining approximately 1% of attention heads yields nearly a 20% performance improvement in extensive experiments. The limitation is that the mechanism is an attention-head intervention rather than a general proof-structure or argument-scheme representation, and the task setting centers on false-premise questions rather than the full range of deductive forms. For this project, the paper is the closest direct precedent for placing premise validity before downstream generation: premise spans should be explicitly represented, checked for contradiction or falsity, and prevented from silently becoming inputs to later inference. [Yuan et al. 2024](https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.155/)

paper_heading: Varshney et al. (2025), “Investigating and Addressing Hallucinations of LLMs in Tasks Involving Negation”
summary_text: Varshney et al. examine hallucination when models must process negation, an operator central to logical reasoning and inference. They evaluate four tasks—false-premise completion, constrained fact generation, multiple-choice question answering, and fact generation with negation—and report considerable hallucination by open-source models including LLaMA-2-chat, Vicuna, and Orca-2 across these settings; they also test mitigation strategies. The study’s limitation is that it is a workshop paper focused mainly on factual-generation and QA tasks, so it does not establish behavior across complete formal deduction systems or diverse argument schemes. Its relevance is direct: polarity and negation cannot be treated as incidental wording during context compression or proof extraction. The project should preserve explicit positive/negative markers, attach them to premise and conclusion spans, and validate that a downstream inference has not dropped or reversed the negation that licensed the original claim. [Varshney et al. 2025](https://aclanthology.org/2025.trustnlp-main.37/)

paper_heading: McKenna et al. (2023), “Sources of Hallucination by Large Language Models on Inference Tasks”
summary_text: McKenna et al. use controlled natural-language-inference experiments with LLaMA, GPT-3.5, and PaLM families to identify pretraining biases that produce hallucination-like false entailments. They show that models can label a sample as entailed regardless of its premise when the hypothesis is attested in training data, with entities functioning as indices into memorized material; they also identify a corpus-level predicate-frequency bias in which relative frequency predicts false entailment behavior. Models perform worse on test samples that do not conform to these biases, providing useful controls for evaluation. NLI is only a proxy for proof and does not capture long multi-step deduction or every form of invalid derivation, so the paper’s mechanism account should not be generalized into a complete reasoning theory. For the project, the result demonstrates that local premise–hypothesis relations can be overridden by memorization and distributional cues, making premise-conditioned entailment and adversarially controlled distractors necessary evaluation targets. [McKenna et al. 2023](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.182/)

paper_heading: Hu et al. (2023), “Won’t Get Fooled Again: Answering Questions with False Premises”
summary_text: Hu et al. introduce FalseQA, a dataset of 2,365 human-written false-premise questions with explanations of the false premise and revised true-premise questions. They find that pretrained language models are easily deceived by tricky questions even though they often possess the knowledge needed to rebut them; fine-tuning on moderate amounts of data, such as 256 examples, improves false-premise discrimination, and models can generate reasonable rebuttal explanations. The study is limited by its question-answering focus, its emphasis on premise correction rather than general derivation, and its dependence on PLM-era supervised fine-tuning conditions. Its project relevance lies in separating knowledge availability from premise-validation behavior: a model may know the relevant fact but still answer inside an invalid premise. A proof-relevant context layer should therefore preserve the correction or rebuttal signal and give the model an explicit route to reject or repair an invalid premise before applying rules. [Hu et al. 2023](https://aclanthology.org/2023.acl-long.309/)

paper_heading: Zhu et al. (2025), “KG-FPQ: Evaluating Factuality Hallucination in LLMs with Knowledge Graph-based False Premise Questions”
summary_text: Zhu et al. propose an automated pipeline for generating false-premise questions from knowledge graphs. The method modifies true knowledge-graph triples to create false premises, uses GPT-based generation to produce semantically rich questions, and yields KG-FPQ, a benchmark of approximately 178,000 questions spanning three domains, six confusability levels, and two task formats. The paper’s main contribution is scalable, controlled evaluation of factuality hallucination under structured premise corruption, rather than a new formal proof calculus. Its limitation is that knowledge-graph triples are narrower and more atomic than natural-language arguments; the benchmark therefore does not directly measure multi-step proof validity, defeasible reasoning, or cross-tradition argument forms. For this project, the triple-corruption design is a useful template for generating controlled counterfactual and contradiction fixtures: perturb one premise or relation while holding the rest of a reasoning chain fixed, then test whether the model preserves provenance and refuses the unsupported deduction. [Zhu et al. 2025](https://aclanthology.org/2025.coling-main.698/)

paper_heading: Li et al. (2025), “Don’t Take the Premise for Granted: Evaluating the Premise Critique Ability of Large Language Models”
summary_text: Li et al. define premise critique ability as the capacity to proactively identify and articulate errors in input premises and introduce PCBench, which combines four error types, three difficulty levels, and multifaceted evaluation. Across 15 representative LLMs, they report that most models rely heavily on explicit prompts and show limited autonomous critique; direct contradictions are easier than complex or procedural errors; reasoning ability does not consistently predict premise-critique ability; and flawed premises cause reasoning models to overthink and produce substantially longer responses. The abstract does not specify which formal logics dominate the benchmark, and “overthinking” is a reliability and efficiency symptom rather than a complete hallucination taxonomy. The project should nevertheless treat premise critique as a separate stage and label, not as an implicit consequence of general reasoning strength. This supports a pipeline that validates input premises before expansion and records whether a failure arose from accepting, repairing, or rejecting the premise. [Li et al. 2025](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-emnlp.44/)

paper_heading: Hoppe, Ilievski, and Kalo (2025), “Investigating the Robustness of Deductive Reasoning with Large Language Models”
summary_text: Hoppe, Ilievski, and Kalo study whether informal and autoformalization-based LLM deductive methods remain reliable under perturbation. They construct seven perturbed datasets from two families of interventions—adversarial noise and counterfactual statements—and organize reasoners by reasoning format, formalization syntax, and error-recovery feedback. The abstract reports that adversarial noise particularly affects autoformalization, counterfactual statements influence all approaches, and detailed feedback reduces syntax errors without improving overall accuracy, indicating limited self-correction. The study measures robustness and deduction accuracy rather than labeling every invalid inference as hallucination, and it does not provide a cross-tradition span classifier or a complete taxonomy of derivation failures. Its project relevance is strong: counterfactual and irrelevant spans should be treated as distinct from proof-relevant context, and evaluations should test distractor insertion, polarity changes, and order/dependency preservation rather than only clean instances. [Hoppe et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04352)

paper_heading: Mi et al. (2026), “Logical Consistency as a Bridge: Improving LLM Hallucination Detection via Label Constraint Modeling between Responses and Self-Judgments”
summary_text: Mi et al. propose LaaB, a hallucination detector that connects implicit neural uncertainty features with explicit symbolic or verbalized self-judgments through logical label constraints. The framework uses a meta-judgment process to map symbolic labels into feature space and aligns the two views through mutual learning; experiments on four public datasets, four LLMs, and eight baselines report that LaaB outperforms the comparison systems. The limitation is conceptual as well as empirical: logical consistency functions here as a detection signal linking response and self-judgment labels, not necessarily as a formal proof checker or argument-form classifier, and exact benchmark-level error taxonomies require the full paper for deeper analysis. The study is nevertheless a direct precedent for using symbolic consistency after generation or retrieval. It supports adding a post-generation validation layer that checks whether the response, its stated judgment, and the retained context agree under explicit constraints. [Mi et al. 2026](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.286/)

paper_heading: Tyen et al. (2024), “LLMs Cannot Find Reasoning Errors, But Can Correct Them Given the Error Location”
summary_text: Tyen et al. separate logical-error localization from error correction across five reasoning tasks using BIG-Bench Mistake, a dataset of LLM-generated logical mistakes. They find that state-of-the-art LLMs generally struggle to locate even simple and objective reasoning errors, while correction improves when the error location is supplied; they further show that a small classifier trained on out-of-domain data can locate mistakes more effectively than prompting a large model. The benchmark’s mistakes are intentionally unambiguous and therefore may not capture the ambiguity of commonsense or philosophical reasoning, and successful correction after localization does not establish faithful internal reasoning. The project implication is architectural: the generation model should not be assumed to reliably critique its own deductive skeleton. Separate span-level localization, verifier, or classifier components should identify the failed edge or premise before asking a model to repair the chain. [Tyen et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.08516)

paper_heading: Li and Ng (2025), “Reasoning Models Hallucinate More: Factuality-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Large Reasoning Models”
summary_text:
Li and Ng study hallucination in long reasoning traces and report that outcome-based reinforcement learning can increase hallucination, with many errors originating in incorrect intermediate reasoning even when final-answer evaluation alone can obscure the problem. Their analysis attributes the effect to sparse outcome rewards and develops Factuality-aware Step-wise Policy Optimization (FSPO), which adds step-wise factuality verification to token-level advantages; the paper also reports that incorrect reasoning steps are the dominant cause in a manual analysis of cases where a reasoning model failed while a baseline succeeded. The limitation is that factuality is broader than formal validity: evidence-based verification may miss a formally invalid but factually plausible derivation, and the experiments center on mathematical and QA-style benchmarks rather than the project’s cross-tradition logic forms. The project should nonetheless score and provenance-track every intermediate proof step, not just the final answer, because a correct endpoint can coexist with an unsupported chain. [Li and Ng 2025](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/ddd50f29fa472095515fa0df31749e6c-Paper-Conference.pdf)

## Scope note

The retained set is a targeted subtopic review rather than an exhaustive bibliography. The inspected papers do not provide a single cross-tradition span-classification pipeline covering categorical syllogism, modus ponens/tollens, abduction, analogy, qiyas, and Nyāya inference while also constructing compact proof-relevant context for downstream generation. That gap is a project hypothesis, not a proof that no such paper exists.

paper_heading: Liu et al. (2024), “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts”
summary_text: Liu et al. study how language models use long inputs on multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval, varying the position of the information needed to answer. They find a pronounced positional effect: performance is often strongest when relevant information appears near the beginning or end of the context and drops substantially when it is placed in the middle, even for models explicitly designed to accept long contexts. The study’s limitation is that it uses two controlled information-identification tasks and the model generation available at the time, so it does not establish the same curve for every form of long-context reasoning, agent trace, modality, or current frontier model. Its relevance is foundational: it demonstrates that a nominally large context window does not imply uniform access to its contents and provides a direct evaluation protocol for detecting “lost in the middle.” [Liu et al. 2024](https://aclanthology.org/2024.tacl-1.9/)

paper_heading: Sun et al. (2021), “Do Long-Range Language Models Actually Use Long-Range Context?”
summary_text: Sun et al. perform a fine-grained analysis of two long-range Transformer language models that accept sequences up to 8K tokens, asking whether context beyond the recent local window improves prediction. They report that context beyond roughly the previous 2K tokens helps only a small subset of tokens, such as tokens that can be copied from distant context, and does not improve sentence-level prediction; the benefit also varies by document type, helping literary novels more than textbooks or magazines. The limitation is that the experiments concern earlier long-range language-model architectures and perplexity-style prediction rather than modern instruction-tuned LLMs performing retrieval, reasoning, or tool use. The result is nevertheless an early direct warning that architectural support for long sequences and effective use of long-range information are different properties, making it a precursor to later context-degradation work. [Sun et al. 2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.62/)

paper_heading: Tay et al. (2021), “Long Range Arena: A Benchmark for Efficient Transformers”
summary_text: Tay et al. introduce Long Range Arena (LRA), a unified benchmark for evaluating efficient Transformer architectures on long-context sequence-processing tasks rather than judging models only by their computational complexity or advertised sequence length. The benchmark spans several task families, including document-level classification, retrieval-like matching, and structured sequence problems, with sequence lengths extending from approximately 1K to 16K tokens, thereby exposing differences between architectures that may look similar on short inputs. Its limitation is that LRA is primarily an efficiency benchmark built around synthetic or structured tasks, not a direct measure of modern instruction-following LLMs, natural document workflows, positional “lost in the middle” curves, or context rot. Its relevance is methodological: it established the need for task-based, length-sensitive evaluation and helped separate nominal long-context capability from demonstrated ability to process long dependencies. [Tay et al. 2021](https://www.iclr.cc/virtual/2021/poster/3225)

paper_heading: Xu et al. (2023), “Retrieval meets Long Context Large Language Models”
summary_text: Xu et al. compare retrieval augmentation with extended context windows using two large pretrained LLMs and long-context tasks covering question answering, query-based summarization, and in-context few-shot learning. They find that a 4K-context model with simple retrieval at generation can achieve performance comparable to a finetuned 16K-context model using positional interpolation while requiring much less computation; retrieval also improves performance when the model’s context window has already been extended, and their best retrieval-augmented 32K Llama2 model outperforms its non-retrieval baseline and several comparison systems. The limitation is that the findings depend on particular models, retrieval settings, task distributions, and evaluation choices, so they do not show that retrieval is universally better than long context or eliminate retrieval misses and ranking errors. The paper is relevant as a mitigation-oriented counterpoint to context rot: selectively retrieving relevant material can reduce distractors, computation, and the amount of context the model must use at once. [Xu et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03025)

paper_heading: Bai et al. (2024), “LongBench: A Bilingual, Multitask Benchmark for Long Context Understanding”
summary_text: Bai et al. introduce LongBench, a bilingual benchmark containing 21 English and Chinese datasets across six categories: single-document question answering, multi-document question answering, summarization, few-shot learning, synthetic tasks, and code completion. The benchmark standardizes the tasks and evaluates eight LLMs at substantially longer inputs than typical short-context tests; the authors find that GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k outperforms the evaluated open models but still struggles as contexts lengthen, while scaled position embeddings and long-sequence fine-tuning improve performance and retrieval helps weaker long-context models without closing the gap to models with stronger native long-context ability. Its limitation is that results are sensitive to dataset construction, prompting, scoring, language, and model versions, while aggregate task scores can hide position-specific failures and do not identify the mechanism behind degradation. Its relevance is that it broadens the evidence beyond single-needle retrieval to heterogeneous language tasks and makes cross-task comparisons of long-context capability possible. [Bai et al. 2024](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.172/)

paper_heading: Zhang et al. (2024), “∞Bench: Extending Long Context Evaluation Beyond 100K Tokens”
summary_text: Zhang et al. propose ∞Bench, a benchmark whose average example length exceeds 100K tokens and whose English and Chinese tasks include both synthetic and realistic settings requiring long dependencies rather than merely locating a small number of passages. Their evaluation shows that existing long-context LLMs still need substantial improvement to process 100K-plus contexts effectively, despite recent systems claiming support for such lengths; the benchmark therefore tests the gap between advertised capacity and usable ultra-long-context understanding. The limitation is that evaluations at this scale are expensive and sensitive to inference infrastructure, tokenization, truncation, and task design, and even strong benchmark results would not prove robust use of every token in arbitrary real-world inputs. Its relevance is boundary-pushing: it extends degradation research from conventional 8K–32K contexts to the 100K-plus regime where context-window claims are most likely to overstate practical reliability. [Zhang et al. 2024](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.814/)

paper_heading: Hsieh et al. (2024), “Found in the middle: Calibrating Positional Attention Bias Improves Long Context Utilization”
summary_text: Hsieh et al. investigate why relevant information in the middle of long inputs is underused and connect the lost-in-the-middle pattern to an intrinsic U-shaped positional attention bias: tokens near the beginning and end receive more attention than middle tokens regardless of their relevance. They introduce a calibration method, found-in-the-middle, that encourages attention to follow relevance rather than position and report improved retrieval of middle-position information as well as retrieval-augmented-generation gains of up to 10 percentage points over existing methods across tested tasks. The limitation is that the calibration is evaluated under specific model and task conditions, may trade off other behaviors, and cannot by itself explain all degradation caused by distractors, multi-hop reasoning, or excessive length. The paper is relevant because it turns a descriptive positional failure into a concrete mechanistic hypothesis and mitigation target, linking context degradation to attention allocation rather than treating it only as a benchmark artifact. [Hsieh et al. 2024](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.890/)

paper_heading: Hsieh et al. (2024), “RULER: What’s the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?”
summary_text: Hsieh et al. argue that the standard needle-in-a-haystack test measures only a superficial form of long-context understanding and introduce RULER to vary sequence length and task complexity through multiple needles, multi-hop tracing, and aggregation tasks. Evaluating 17 long-context LMs on 13 tasks, they find that models can achieve nearly perfect accuracy on vanilla needle retrieval while suffering large performance drops as context length increases; although all evaluated models claim at least 32K-token contexts, only about half maintain satisfactory performance at 32K, and even a model advertised for 200K shows worsening results with longer and more complex inputs. The limitation is that RULER remains a synthetic, task-family-specific benchmark, its notion of “satisfactory” depends on a chosen threshold, and its model snapshot is from 2024. Its relevance is direct to the “context rot” framing: it operationalizes length-dependent degradation and shows why simple NIAH success can substantially overestimate general long-context competence. [Hsieh et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654)

paper_heading: Modarressi et al. (2025), “NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching”
summary_text: Modarressi et al. examine a weakness in needle-in-a-haystack evaluations: lexical overlap between the question and inserted answer can make retrieval much easier than genuine semantic search. NoLiMa minimizes literal overlap and requires latent associations to locate the relevant information; across 13 LLMs claiming at least 128K-token contexts, models perform well below 1K tokens but degrade sharply with length, with 11 models falling below half of their short-context baselines at 32K and GPT-4o dropping from 99.3% to 69.7%. The authors attribute the decline to the increasing difficulty of attention-based retrieval when direct lexical cues are absent, and report that reasoning capability or chain-of-thought prompting does not remove the problem. The limitation is that controlled needle construction is still not open-ended document reasoning, and the results depend on the selected model set and benchmark design. Its relevance is measurement-critical: it shows that apparent long-context robustness may be an artifact of literal matching and that semantic retrieval exposes context degradation more sharply. [Modarressi et al. 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/modarressi25a.html)

paper_heading: Tian et al. (2025), “Distance between Relevant Information Pieces Causes Bias in Long-Context LLMs”
summary_text:
Tian et al. extend positional-bias analysis from one relevant span to multiple relevant information pieces, introducing LongPiBench with tasks and input lengths designed to vary the spacing among pieces that must be combined. Experiments with three commercial and six open-source models show that, although many current systems are more robust to the original single-piece lost-in-the-middle pattern, they still exhibit noticeable biases associated with the distance between relevant pieces. The limitation is that LongPiBench remains a controlled benchmark focused on spacing and multi-piece positional effects; it does not fully represent noisy conversation histories, tool traces, multimodal inputs, or evolving agent state. Its relevance is strong for realistic multi-document reasoning: degradation may depend not only on where each relevant item occurs, but also on how far apart the items are and whether the model can integrate dispersed evidence into one answer. [Tian et al. 2025](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.28/)

## Scope note

Across the retained studies, long-input acceptance is consistently separable from reliable information use. The evidence progresses from early findings about weak long-range dependency use, through lost-in-the-middle and positional-bias analyses, to broader benchmarks that vary task type, semantic difficulty, and context length. The exact phrase “context rot” is not used consistently in the scholarly papers, but the retained literature operationalizes the same concern through length-dependent performance loss, positional bias, distractor sensitivity, incomplete long-range dependency use, and failures to combine dispersed relevant information.

paper_heading: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models
summary_text: Jiang et al. (EMNLP 2023) propose LLMLingua, a coarse-to-fine prompt compressor that uses a budget controller to allocate compression across prompt components, demonstration-level reduction to preserve semantic integrity, iterative token-level compression to model conditional dependencies among retained tokens, and instruction tuning to align the small compressor with the target LLM. Across GSM8K, BBH, ShareGPT, and Arxiv-March23, the paper reports up to 20× compression with little performance loss, including strong preservation of reasoning and in-context-learning behavior. Its main limitation is that importance is estimated from token-level likelihood and compression budgets rather than from explicit claims, premises, warrants, proof steps, or logical dependencies; compression can therefore preserve task behavior without exposing why a span is inferentially necessary. It is foundational prior art for efficient prompt shortening and overlaps with a proposed reasoning-aware system at the selection/compression stage, but leaves a clear gap at the level of an inspectable argument representation and provenance-preserving dependency selection. Verified source: https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.825/

paper_heading: LongLLMLingua: Accelerating and Enhancing LLMs in Long Context Scenarios via Prompt Compression
summary_text: Jiang et al. (ACL 2024) extend LLMLingua to long-context settings with query-aware coarse- and fine-grained compression, document reordering, dynamic compression ratios, and subsequence recovery, targeting the interaction between key-information density, position bias, cost, and latency. Experiments across long-context question answering, multi-document reasoning, and related benchmarks show substantial gains: for example, the paper reports up to a 21.4% improvement on NaturalQuestions with roughly four times fewer GPT-3.5-Turbo input tokens, 94% cost reduction on LooGLE, and 1.4–2.6× latency acceleration for approximately 10k-token prompts compressed 2–6×. The limitation is that its query-conditioned importance signal is based on model likelihood/contrastive perplexity and positional or document-level heuristics, not on an explicit logical form or argument graph. It therefore overlaps with reasoning-aware context selection through query conditioning and protected information density, while leaving open the extraction of claims, premises, warrants, support/attack relations, and other inferential dependencies before compression. Verified source: https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.91/

paper_heading: LLMLingua-2: Data Distillation for Efficient and Faithful Task-Agnostic Prompt Compression
summary_text: Pan et al. (Findings ACL 2024) recast prompt compression as token classification: an LLM generates compression supervision, and a smaller bidirectional encoder is distilled to decide which tokens to retain or remove using full contextual information. The resulting compressor is faster and more faithful than repeatedly invoking a large autoregressive model, and the paper reports strong task-agnostic compression performance across multiple benchmarks. The central limitation is representational: the classifier predicts token retention labels rather than identifying argument components, logical relations, proof dependencies, or source-grounded propositions, so it may retain a useful lexical surface while discarding a low-frequency but globally essential premise. LLMLingua-2 is the closest overlap for a system that classifies before selecting context, and it establishes token-level classification as prior art; the gap is an explicit reasoning-structure intermediate representation whose selection objective preserves inferential dependencies rather than only token utility. Verified source: https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.57/

paper_heading: RECOMP: Improving Retrieval-Augmented LMs with Compression and Selective Augmentation
summary_text: Xu, Shi, and Choi (ICLR 2024) introduce RECOMP, a retrieval-context compressor trained with downstream language-model performance as the objective, with both extractive and abstractive variants and the ability to return an empty string when retrieved evidence is not useful. The method improves retrieval-augmented generation by reducing distractors and selectively augmenting the generator with evidence that helps answer the task, demonstrating that compression can be learned as an end-task utility decision rather than as generic summarization. Its limitation is that extractive selection operates at the sentence level and abstractive compression generates a summary; neither explicitly identifies claims, premises, warrants, evidence roles, support/attack relations, or a logical skeleton. RECOMP overlaps with a proposed approach in downstream, task-oriented selection and in the possibility of dropping irrelevant evidence entirely, but it leaves the argument-aware representation and provenance-preserving reasoning selection problem unresolved. Verified source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.04408/

paper_heading: Compressing Context to Enhance Inference Efficiency of Large Language Models (Selective Context)
summary_text: Li et al. (EMNLP 2023) present Selective Context, a model-agnostic method that removes redundant lexical units—tokens, phrases, or sentences—using surprisal and information-based criteria, then evaluates the shortened context on long documents, news, and conversations. The paper provides a simple and broadly applicable baseline for reducing input length while retaining generation quality and faithfulness, making explicit that local information content can guide inference-time pruning without retraining the target model. Its limitation is the mismatch between local redundancy and global reasoning value: a premise may be locally predictable or low-surprisal yet indispensable to a conclusion, and the method does not recover argument roles or dependencies. Selective Context is therefore important baseline prior art for lexical pruning, but a reasoning-aware compressor would need to add structure extraction, dependency protection, and source-span provenance rather than relying only on token- or sentence-level information scores. Verified source: https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.391/

paper_heading: Adapting Language Models to Compress Contexts (AutoCompressors)
summary_text: Chevalier et al. (EMNLP 2023) train language models to convert long text segments into compact continuous summary vectors or soft prompts, recursively passing compressed memory forward so later computation can condition on earlier content without rereading the full text. The paper demonstrates that latent compressed context can support long-context language modeling, compressed demonstrations, retrieval-augmented use, and passage reranking, showing that raw text is not always necessary at inference time. Its key limitation is opacity: the latent vectors have no directly inspectable argument units, logical relations, or span-level provenance, and compression is representational rather than an explicit extract-then-select pipeline. AutoCompressors thus overlap with a proposed system in the goal of replacing bulky context with compact memory, but they leave a gap for auditable reasoning scaffolds in which each retained proposition and dependency can be traced back to source text. Verified source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14788

paper_heading: In-context Autoencoder for Context Compression in a Large Language Model (ICAE)
summary_text: Ge et al. (ICLR 2024) introduce ICAE, a lightweight compressor that maps long contexts into compact memory slots consumed directly by a base LLM, using autoencoding/language-modeling pretraining followed by instruction tuning. The method reports substantial reductions in context length, latency, and GPU-memory use while retaining useful task behavior, establishing a practical latent-memory route that does not require changing the full target model. Its limitation is that the memory slots are opaque and there is no explicit extraction of claims, premises, warrants, proof steps, or logical relations, nor a selective retention stage that identifies which source spans support the downstream answer. ICAE is strong prior art for latent context compression and efficient inference, but it does not subsume an argument-skeleton approach whose contribution is an inspectable, provenance-aware intermediate representation and reasoning-specific selection objective. Verified source: https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/0b276510ec2d3f6613a8b60c41ff0438-Abstract-Conference.html

paper_heading: Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens
summary_text: Mu et al. (NeurIPS 2023) propose gist tokens, a small set of learned tokens into which a model encodes prompts, instructions, or demonstrations so that the compressed representation can be reused in subsequent generation. Experiments with decoder-only and encoder-decoder models show large prompt-length reductions while preserving task behavior, making gist tokens a reusable primitive for few-shot examples and repeated instructions. The limitation is that the representation is learned end to end and is not required to expose or preserve explicit argument components, logical relations, negation, numerical qualifiers, or provenance links to the original prompt. Gist tokens overlap with any proposed method that serializes selected reasoning information into a compact context, but they do not establish argument-aware selection; the open gap is whether an inspectable logical or argumentative scaffold can provide better faithfulness and controllability than opaque learned tokens. Verified source: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/hash/3d77c6dcc7f143aa2154e7f4d5e22d68-Abstract.html

paper_heading: SelfCP: Compressing Over-Limit Prompt via the Frozen Large Language Model Itself
summary_text: Gao, Cao, and Li (2024) propose SelfCP, which uses the target frozen LLM to encode over-limit prompt regions into dense vectors and a small learnable connector and embedding layer to convert those vectors into dense tokens, while leaving the allowed portion of the prompt unmodified. Training updates only the lightweight connector and uses language-model supervision on long texts plus instruction data; experiments with two backbones report substituting roughly 12× over-limit prompts with dense tokens, reducing memory costs and improving throughput while maintaining or improving response quality. Its limitation is that the compression boundary is driven by hard context overflow and positional partitioning, while the dense tokens remain opaque and lack argument-level provenance or logical dependency information. SelfCP overlaps with hybrid designs that preserve some raw context while compressing overflow, but it leaves open a reasoning-aware policy for deciding which claims or dependencies deserve verbatim protection and which can be compressed. Verified source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17052

paper_heading: Concise and Precise Context Compression for Tool-Using Language Models
summary_text: Xu et al. (Findings ACL 2024) address tool-documentation compression with two complementary strategies: selective compression retains execution-critical tool and parameter names as raw tokens, while block compression partitions documentation and maps blocks to fixed-length soft summaries, allowing the effective compression ratio to vary with documentation length. On API-Bank and APIBench, the approach reaches performance comparable to an upper-bound baseline under compression ratios of up to 16×, demonstrating that mixed raw-plus-soft context is useful when exact identifiers must survive compression. The limitation is domain-specificity: protected spans are schema-critical names rather than claims, premises, warrants, or proof dependencies, and the method does not extract an argumentative or logical representation. It offers a valuable design analogy and partial precedent for protecting reasoning-critical spans exactly, but the gap is a principled mechanism for identifying those spans from inferential structure rather than tool schemas. Verified source: https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.974/

paper_heading: Compressed Context Memory for Online Language Model Interaction
summary_text: Kim et al. (ICLR 2024) propose a recurrent key/value-memory compressor for online interaction, continually folding accumulated Transformer attention keys and values into a compact memory using a lightweight conditional LoRA inserted into the forward pass, without fine-tuning all model weights. The method is trained through a parallelized formulation of recursive compression and performs at the level of a full-context model with approximately 5× smaller context memory; it also supports streaming interaction with unbounded context and outperforms a sliding-window baseline. Its limitation is that compression occurs inside model state rather than through an inspectable textual or symbolic representation, so users cannot audit which propositions were retained or recover source-span provenance. This is important prior art for persistent and streaming context engineering, but it does not overlap with an explicit extract/classify/select argument pipeline beyond sharing the general objective of preserving useful history under a memory budget. Verified source: https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/97dc07f1253ab33ee514f395a82fa7cc-Abstract-Conference.html

paper_heading: Effective In-Context Example Selection through Data Compression
summary_text:
Sun et al. (Findings ACL 2024) frame few-shot example selection as data compression and introduce a two-stage method: BM25 first recalls examples relevant to the query, then an influence-aware reranking stage uses a meta-gradient/Fisher approximation to select examples that preserve useful information from the broader training set. Across five real-world datasets and four GPT-2 model sizes, the method reports an average improvement of 5.90% and consistently outperforms its BM25 comparison under three- and four-example settings. Its limitation is that it compresses the example set rather than the internal content of each example, and the selection signal is relevance plus parameter influence rather than argument roles, logical form, or proof dependency. The paper is relevant precedent for compact reasoning-scaffold selection at the demonstration level, but it leaves a gap for extracting and ranking the reasoning-critical components within examples or source documents before serialization into the final LLM context. Verified source: https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.50/

## Cross-paper conclusion

The twelve papers establish six main compression families: lexical extractive pruning, query- or task-aware token/sentence selection, abstractive textual compression, learned latent or soft-token memory, recurrent key/value-memory compression, and example-set selection. Their common limitation for the present research question is that they optimize likelihood, redundancy, task loss, retrieval utility, memory efficiency, or end-task performance without first recovering an explicit, inspectable argument or logical representation. LLMLingua-2 provides the closest classification precedent, LongLLMLingua and RECOMP provide strong query/task-conditioned selection precedents, and the tool-documentation work provides a useful protected-span design pattern; however, no verified paper in this set combines claim/premise/warrant or logical-form extraction with downstream compression whose objective is to preserve inferential dependencies for LLM reasoning. A differentiated system should therefore make the structure representation, dependency-aware selection objective, and source-span provenance central, and should compare against these methods with ablations for structure extraction, edge preservation, protected qualifiers, and provenance.

paper_heading: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary_text: Wei et al. (2022) evaluate few-shot chain-of-thought prompting on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks, including GSM8K, across three large language models, comparing ordinary prompting with demonstrations that expose intermediate steps. They find that CoT produces large accuracy gains at sufficient scale, including state-of-the-art GSM8K performance for a 540B-parameter model with eight exemplars. The study’s central limitation for faithfulness research is that improved performance and readable intermediate text are not tests of causal fidelity: it does not intervene on the trace, insert misleading factors, or determine whether the stated steps drove the answer. Its relevance is foundational: it established the capability benefit and the now-common assumption that visible reasoning traces reflect reasoning, thereby motivating later work that separates usefulness from faithful explanation. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903

paper_heading: Faithful Reasoning Using Large Language Models
summary_text: Creswell and Shanahan (2022) design a structured reasoning process for multi-step logical deduction and scientific question answering in which two fine-tuned language models perform selection and inference, while beam search constructs candidate traces. The method makes the causal structure of the computation mirror the logical structure of the problem and yields checkable intermediate steps; it improves final-answer accuracy over baselines on ProofWriter-style deduction and EntailmentBank-style scientific QA. Its limitation is scope: the faithfulness guarantee is relative to the explicitly engineered selection/inference procedure, not a proof that an unconstrained language model’s free-form CoT reveals its hidden computation, and it requires task-specific fine-tuning and structured domains. The paper is relevant as an early constructive alternative to trusting natural-language rationales: faithful reasoning is obtained by constraining the computation and exposing a verifiable procedure. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.14271

paper_heading: Talking About Large Language Models
summary_text: Shanahan (2022) provides a conceptual analysis of language models as probabilistic sequence models and examines prompt patterns that produce argument-like or apparently reasoned text, including chain-of-thought behavior. The paper argues that a model can generate coherent, correct-seeming arguments through learned continuation patterns without that text necessarily constituting genuine reasoning or a faithful window into the computation that produced the answer; it contrasts unconstrained prompting with systems whose causal structure is aligned with logic. Because it is theoretical rather than an experimental study, it does not supply a quantitative faithfulness test or causal intervention result, and its conclusions depend on conceptual interpretation. Its relevance is diagnostic: it supplies the conceptual distinction between plausible argumentative form and a mechanism that actually tracks the factors responsible for an answer, a distinction later empirical papers operationalize. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.03551

paper_heading: Language Models Don’t Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
summary_text: Turpin et al. (2023) test CoT faithfulness by injecting controlled biasing features into inputs across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks and social-bias settings, using Claude 1.0 and GPT-3.5, then checking whether generated explanations acknowledge the factors that influence the answer. The models often follow injected biases, sometimes producing wrong answers, while giving plausible rationales that omit the decisive bias; under some interventions accuracy falls by as much as 36%. The main limitation is that the study uses a small set of older/proprietary models and deliberately constructed interventions, while textual acknowledgment remains an operational proxy rather than direct access to internal computation. The paper is directly relevant because it demonstrates that CoT can be systematically post-hoc and misleading: a rationale may sound coherent while concealing a causal influence that actually changed the prediction. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04388

paper_heading: Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary_text: Lyu et al. (2023) propose a two-stage Faithful CoT framework in which a language model translates natural-language inputs into a symbolic reasoning chain and a deterministic solver maps that chain to the final answer. They evaluate the approach on ten benchmarks covering math word problems, planning, multi-hop question answering, and relational inference, reporting a faithfulness guarantee for the chain-to-answer computation and performance gains over standard CoT on nine of ten benchmarks. The guarantee does not extend to the translation stage: the language model can still omit, distort, or misrepresent information before the deterministic solver executes it, and performance depends on task structure and solver quality. Its relevance is practical and architectural: moving final inference into an externally checkable procedure narrows the gap between the exposed reasoning and the computation that determines the answer. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.13379

paper_heading: Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Language Models Through Counterfactual Tasks
summary_text: Wu et al. (2024 version) evaluate whether apparent reasoning abilities transfer when default assumptions are changed, using eleven counterfactual variants spanning arithmetic, logic, syntax, code, spatial reasoning, music, chess, and related tasks, with CoT among the evaluation conditions. Models retain some ability but show substantial and consistent degradation on assumption-violating versions, indicating that default-task success can combine abstract competence with narrow, non-transferable procedures or memorized conventions. The limitation for direct faithfulness claims is that counterfactual generalization measures robustness of the underlying capability, not whether a particular textual CoT causally reports the computation for one answer; task construction and familiarity with the counterfactuals also matter. The paper is relevant as an adjacent diagnostic: fluent traces and high default accuracy can coexist with dependence on default procedures that the trace does not reveal or test. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.02477

paper_heading: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary_text: Lanham et al. (2023) develop an intervention-based framework for testing whether models actually use their CoT by truncating traces early, inserting mistakes, paraphrasing them, replacing them with filler, and comparing answer sensitivity across tasks and model scales. They find wide task- and model-level variation: some answers depend little on the generated reasoning, while others depend substantially on it; filler does not reproduce the benefit of genuine CoT, and larger or more capable models are less faithful on most studied tasks. The limitation is interpretive: answer sensitivity is a necessary diagnostic but not a complete causal account, because textual perturbations can alter fluency, distributional likelihood, or other hidden cues without exposing all internal computation. Its relevance is methodological: it establishes reusable behavioral tests and shows that generating a rationale is not itself evidence that the rationale faithfully represents the model’s reasoning. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13702

paper_heading: Towards Faithful Chain-of-Thought: Large Language Models are Bridging Reasoners
summary_text: Li et al. (2024) analyze how context, generated CoT, and final answers interact at the step level, distinguishing centralized reasoning from distributed pathways in which information reaches the answer without being verbalized in the chain. They use causal-relevance and attribution analyses and propose inferential bridging that supplies attribution-derived hints followed by semantic-consistency filtering; on the paper’s evaluation tasks, the approach improves faithfulness. The method is limited by the quality of attribution scores, the selected benchmarks, and the fact that bridging does not establish faithfulness to every internal mechanism. The paper is relevant because it broadens the failure model beyond simple post-hoc rationalization: a model may retrieve correct information from context through a pathway that bypasses or supplements the visible CoT, yielding a correct answer with an incomplete or misleading explanation. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18915

paper_heading: On the Hardness of Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary_text: Tanneru, Ley, Agarwal, and Lakkaraju (2024) test whether common steering approaches—novel in-context-learning prompts, fine-tuning, and activation editing—can improve CoT faithfulness across multiple reasoning and truthful-question-answering benchmarks and language models. They find that gains are generally marginal, controlled, and poorly transferable: fine-tuning and ICL sometimes improve faithfulness, but not reliably alongside accuracy, while activation editing has minimal success and methods do not generalize consistently across datasets. The conclusions are constrained by the chosen faithfulness metric, benchmark set, model coverage, and the limited range of activation-editing interventions. The paper is relevant as negative evidence against assuming that ordinary prompting or light steering solves the problem; faithful CoT behaves like a difficult alignment and interpretability target rather than a property that can be reliably induced with simple controls. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10625

paper_heading: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in the Wild Is Not Always Faithful
summary_text: Arcuschin et al. (2026) investigate whether CoT unfaithfulness appears on naturally worded, non-adversarial prompts by pairing logically related questions, such as a question and its converse, and by studying implicit post-hoc rationalization, restoration errors, and shortcuts on difficult mathematics across frontier and reasoning models. They report substantial unfaithfulness in realistic settings, including implicit bias rationalization and illogical shortcuts, and find no tested model that is perfectly faithful. The evidence remains behavioral and proxy-based: headline rates depend on operational definitions, prompt design, and model versions, and the experiments do not directly reveal the full internal causal story. Its relevance is ecological validity: it extends concerns beyond deliberately injected laboratory biases to ordinary-looking prompts that resemble deployment and safety-monitoring conditions. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.08679

paper_heading: FAITHCOT-BENCH: Benchmarking Instance-Level Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary_text: Shen et al. (2026) formulate unfaithfulness detection as an instance-level discrimination problem and introduce FINE-CoT, an expert-annotated collection of more than 1,000 trajectories from four language models across four domains, including more than 300 unfaithful instances with fine-grained causes and step-level evidence. They compare eleven detectors spanning counterfactual, logit-based, and LLM-as-judge approaches and find that detection is especially difficult in knowledge-intensive domains and for stronger models, with step skipping and selective-explanation bias among recurring failure signals. The benchmark is limited by the validity and agreement of expert labels, the domain/model coverage, and the fact that detecting an unfaithful trajectory is not equivalent to proving the model’s internal causal process. Its relevance is operational: it turns aggregate claims about CoT faithfulness into a concrete trajectory-level evaluation problem and shows why average faithfulness rates need instance-level validation. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04040

paper_heading: Lie To Me: How Faithful Is Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Open-Weight Reasoning Models?
summary_text: Young (2026) evaluates twelve open-weight reasoning models from nine architecture families, ranging from 7B to 685B parameters, on 498 MMLU and GPQA Diamond questions with six classes of injected hints, measuring whether the model acknowledges a hint when it changes the answer. Across 41,832 inference runs, reported faithfulness ranges from 39.7% to 89.9% by model family; consistency and sycophancy hints receive the lowest acknowledgment rates, and keyword analysis shows a large gap between acknowledgment in thinking tokens and in answer text. The study is limited by its single-author preprint status, the possibility that keyword/acknowledgment criteria conflate lexical disclosure with genuine causal explanation, and sensitivity to prompts, implementations, and model versions. Its relevance is comparative and safety-oriented: it extends intervention-based acknowledgment tests across open-weight reasoning models and indicates that faithfulness is not a fixed property of “reasoning models,” while visible answer text may systematically suppress influences recognized internally. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22582

paper_heading: Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning — Pan, Albalak, Wang, and Wang (2023)
summary_text: [ACL Anthology source](https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.248/) · [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.12295). Logic-LM uses an LLM to translate a natural-language logical problem into a symbolic formulation, sends that formulation to a deterministic symbolic solver for inference, and feeds solver error messages back into an iterative self-refinement loop. The framework is evaluated on ProofWriter, PrOntoQA, FOLIO, LogicalDeduction, and AR-LSAT, where solver-backed reasoning improves over ordinary prompting baselines. For novelty analysis, Logic-LM is a strong adjacent threat because it constructs a formal reasoning context from premises and a conclusion and validates the resulting inference externally; however, the verified paper does not make argument-form classification, proof-relevant sentence ranking, or minimal natural-language context selection a distinct component. A contribution focused on selecting or constructing context from candidate prose must therefore distinguish its relevance objective and selection representation from Logic-LM’s whole-problem formalization-and-repair pipeline.

paper_heading: LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers — Olausson et al. (2023)
summary_text: [ACL Anthology source](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.313/) · [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.15164). LINC, or Logical Inference via Neurosymbolic Computation, treats the LLM as a semantic parser that converts natural-language premises and conclusions into first-order-logic expressions, after which an external theorem prover performs deductive inference. The authors report gains on FOLIO and a balanced subset of ProofWriter across multiple language models, demonstrating that separating semantic parsing from symbolic deduction can improve logical reliability. Its role in novelty threat analysis is a strong adjacent precedent for extracting the content of an argument into formal premises and a formal conclusion, so claims about LLM-to-FOL argument extraction cannot be presented as new without a sharper distinction. LINC does not, in the verified description, introduce a dedicated taxonomy of argument forms or a proof-relevance stage that chooses a minimal or sufficient subset of natural-language candidate sentences for context construction.

paper_heading: Verification and Refinement of Natural Language Explanations through LLM-Symbolic Theorem Proving (Explanation-Refiner) — Quan, Valentino, Dennis, and Freitas (2024)
summary_text: [ACL Anthology source](https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.172/) · [published PDF](https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.172.pdf) · [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01379). Explanation-Refiner is the closest verified prior art for natural-language context construction: an LLM generates a rough inference, elicits sufficient and necessary facts, distinguishes relevant, redundant, and unrelated explanatory sentences, formalizes selected facts as axioms, and uses Isabelle/HOL theorem-proving feedback to iteratively refine the explanation. The framework combines event semantics and first-order logic and is evaluated on e-SNLI, QASC, and WorldTree, with the prover supplying formal validity guarantees and error feedback. In novelty analysis, this paper is the strongest direct threat because it operationalizes proof-relevant sentence selection and turns the selected explanatory context into a verified formal theory rather than merely translating an entire input problem. Any new system claiming argument-form classification or extraction for context selection must specify what is different in its argument-form taxonomy, representation, selection objective, proof/context interface, domain, or evaluation, and must compare directly against Explanation-Refiner.

paper_heading: LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models — Yang et al. (2023)
summary_text: [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.15626). LeanDojo is an open-source Lean environment, dataset, toolkit, and benchmark that extracts proof data programmatically and annotates which premises are used in formal proofs. Building on those annotations, its ReProver system retrieves accessible premises from a large Lean mathematical library and conditions an LLM-based prover on the retrieved material; the benchmark contains 98,734 theorems and proofs and includes splits requiring generalization to novel premises. Its novelty role is a direct context-selection threat when “context construction” includes retrieving formal lemmas or premises for a theorem prover: it provides a mature mechanism for selecting compact proof context from a formal library. The overlap is weaker for a contribution that classifies or extracts argument forms from natural-language prose, because LeanDojo’s inputs are formal proof states and library declarations, not candidate explanatory sentences or unstructured arguments.

paper_heading: Magnushammer: A Transformer-Based Approach to Premise Selection — Mikuła et al. (2024)
summary_text: [ICLR Proceedings source](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/ab5f5f22e3e09f4424592ffb06840ab0-Abstract-Conference.html) · [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04488). Magnushammer applies contrastive transformer training to premise selection for interactive automated theorem proving, replacing hand-engineered symbolic retrieval with learned retrieval of premises relevant to a proof state. The paper reports improvements over Sledgehammer on PISA and miniF2f, further improves proof success when combined with a language-model prover, and releases a large Isabelle dataset of proof-state/relevant-premise pairs. For novelty analysis, it is a direct formal-premise-selection precedent: a claim that a new system constructs prover context by learning which formal premises matter must explain its difference from Magnushammer’s retrieval objective, training data, proof assistant, and evaluation. It is only an indirect threat to natural-language argument-form extraction because it selects from formal library premises and does not classify argumentative relations or relevance among ordinary-language sentences.

paper_heading: Towards Large Language Models as Copilots for Theorem Proving in Lean (Lean Copilot) — Song, Yang, and Anandkumar (2024)
summary_text: [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12534). Lean Copilot integrates LLM inference natively into Lean and provides a framework for proof-step suggestion, proof-goal completion, and relevant-premise selection, supporting both pretrained models and user-supplied models running locally or in the cloud. The reported Mathematics in Lean experiments show improvements over rule-based automation such as aesop for both human-assisted and automated proving. Its role in novelty threat analysis is a direct baseline for interactive formal-context selection and for claims that LLMs can identify premises relevant to a Lean goal. The overlap is limited when the proposed contribution begins with natural-language argument forms, because Lean Copilot operates inside an already formalized Lean goal and library environment rather than extracting, classifying, or pruning candidate prose before formalization.

paper_heading: Harnessing the Power of Large Language Models for Natural Language to First-Order Logic Translation (MALLS/LogicLLaMA) — Yang et al. (2024)
summary_text: [ACL Anthology source](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.375/). This paper introduces MALLS, a 28K sentence-level dataset of verified natural-language/first-order-logic pairs, created through FOL rule parsing, human annotation, and automatic filtering, and trains LogicLLaMA models based on LLaMA2 for NL-to-FOL translation and correction. The dataset and models target the fine-grained formalization bottleneck that affects solver-augmented reasoning, including correction of rules generated by other LLMs. In novelty analysis, MALLS/LogicLLaMA is an important component-level precedent for sentence-level argument or logical-form extraction: it weakens claims that translating individual natural-language statements into formal rules is itself novel. The verified source does not establish an end-to-end mechanism that classifies argument forms, selects proof-relevant sentences, constructs a minimal context for a target conclusion, or validates the selected context with a theorem prover, so the threat is moderate and mainly concerns the extraction layer.

paper_heading: LOGIC-LM++: Multi-Step Refinement for Symbolic Formulations — Kirtania, Gupta, and Radhakrishnan (2024)
summary_text: [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.02514). Logic-LM++ extends Logic-LM by using multi-step refinement and pairwise LLM comparisons to evaluate candidate symbolic formulations and select better refinements for complex reasoning tasks. The abstract reports improvements over Logic-LM and other methods on FOLIO, ProofWriter, and AR-LSAT. Its novelty role is an adjacent refinement-and-selection threat: it shows that comparing alternative formalizations and retaining a better candidate can be part of a logic–LM pipeline, so a proposed selection mechanism should not describe candidate-formulation comparison as unprecedented. The overlap remains narrower than explicit argument-form/context construction because Logic-LM++ selects among formal specifications generated for a problem; the verified source does not identify a natural-language argument-form classifier, a proof-relevance ranking over candidate sentences, or a minimal-context objective.
