paper_heading: Automated Theorem Provers Help Improve Large Language Model Reasoning — McGinness and Baumgartner (2024)
summary_text: [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03492) · [LPAR 2024 reference](https://doi.org/10.29007/2n9m). This work uses an LLM as a front end that translates PRONTOQA steamroller problems into a formal logic language, invokes logic-programming systems and first-order automated theorem provers, and analyzes translation failures using syntactic and semantic error categories. Its main extension uses theorem provers to correct semantic translation errors, reducing those errors and improving reasoning accuracy. For novelty analysis, it is a correction and validation precedent: it threatens claims that prover feedback can diagnose or repair faulty formalized arguments, and it establishes the importance of separating translation correctness from downstream proving. The verified paper does not report a dedicated argument-form classifier or a context selector that chooses relevant natural-language facts; its system formalizes the given problem and repairs errors, so the overlap with selective context construction is moderate and indirect.

paper_heading: LeanReasoner: Boosting Complex Logical Reasoning with Lean — Jiang, Fonseca, and Cohen (2024)
summary_text: [ACL Anthology source](https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.416/). LeanReasoner formalizes logical reasoning problems as Lean theorems and solves them by proving or disproving the corresponding formal statements, leveraging Lean’s symbolic checking and theorem library. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on FOLIO and near-state-of-the-art performance on ProofWriter while using fewer than 100 in-domain samples per dataset. Its novelty role is a formal-context and proof-assistant baseline: it shows that converting natural-language logical tasks into a theorem-prover representation and relying on library-backed symbolic verification is established practice. The overlap is weaker for argument-form classification or selective context construction because the abstract describes theorem formalization and proof/disproof rather than a separate stage that extracts argumentative relations, ranks candidate facts, or constructs a minimal proof-relevant context.

paper_heading: Language Models can be Deductive Solvers (LoGiPT) — Feng et al. (2024)
summary_text:
[ACL Anthology source](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-naacl.254/) · [arXiv source](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.06158). LoGiPT addresses a weakness of solver-augmented language models in which an LLM’s parsing error prevents the external solver from executing: instead of relying on an explicit parser-to-solver interface, it trains a language model to internalize and emulate deductive-solver reasoning while adhering to strict solver syntax and grammar. The model is trained on a dataset derived from revealed and refined solver reasoning and is evaluated on two deductive reasoning benchmarks, outperforming solver-augmented and few-shot alternatives in the reported experiments. For novelty analysis, LoGiPT is a weak direct threat to context construction because it intentionally removes the explicit parsing, selection, and external-prover stages; it is nonetheless relevant as an alternative architecture for formal-syntax adherence and logical execution. A system whose novelty depends on explicit argument-form extraction, proof-relevant context selection, or prover-verified construction remains distinguishable from LoGiPT’s end-to-end solver imitation.

## Cross-paper novelty conclusion

The retained literature separates into three context regimes. Explanation-Refiner is the closest precedent for selecting relevant, sufficient, necessary, redundant, and unrelated natural-language facts and converting the selected material into a prover-checked theory. Logic-LM and LINC are the main precedents for converting whole natural-language logical problems into formal premises and conclusions, while MALLS/LogicLLaMA strengthens the sentence-level translation component. LeanDojo/ReProver, Magnushammer, and Lean Copilot are the principal formal-library premise-retrieval precedents. Logic-LM++, Automated Theorem Provers Help Improve LLM Reasoning, LeanReasoner, and LoGiPT cover refinement, correction, Lean formalization, and solver imitation, respectively. A differentiated contribution should therefore state whether its novelty lies in a new argument-form taxonomy, extraction of argumentative relations rather than sentence-level FOL translation, proof-relevance selection under an explicit sufficiency/minimality/coverage/faithfulness objective, a cross-domain or long-context setting, or a new interface from selected natural-language context to formal verification; it should compare directly against Explanation-Refiner, Logic-LM/LINC, and at least one formal-premise retriever.

paper_heading: Johnson-Laird & Bara (1984), “Syllogistic Inference”
summary_text: Johnson-Laird and Bara’s benchmark is a foundational human experimental regime for categorical syllogisms and three-term series problems, varying premise figure—the arrangement of terms—and the number of mental models required by an inference. Their experiments found systematic effects of figure and model count on performance and supported a mental-model account in which reasoners construct a model, derive a candidate conclusion, and search for counterexamples. Its limitation is that it is a small, classical human-cognition study rather than an LLM benchmark, and its theory and stimuli predate contemporary natural-language evaluation protocols. It remains directly relevant because any LLM syllogism benchmark that manipulates term order, figure, validity, or model complexity is extending a test structure already established in this work. Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0010027784900350

paper_heading: Oakhill, Johnson-Laird & Garnham (1989), “Believability and Syllogistic Reasoning”
summary_text: This paper tests belief bias in syllogistic reasoning by examining whether believability affects premise interpretation, the examination of alternative representations, or the final filtering of candidate conclusions. Across three experiments involving both conclusion generation and conclusion evaluation, participants were influenced by beliefs at the alternative-model and conclusion-filtering stages, not only during initial premise interpretation. The limitation is that the evidence concerns human subjects and controlled syllogistic materials, so it does not directly quantify LLM reasoning or distinguish all modern failure modes such as parsing and format errors. Its relevance is methodological: benchmark items should cross logical validity with believable, unbelievable, and neutral content, because an accuracy score alone can hide whether a system is following logic or accepting plausible conclusions. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2721132/

paper_heading: Clark, Tafjord & Richardson (2020), “Transformers as Soft Reasoners over Language” (RuleTaker)
summary_text: RuleTaker evaluates whether transformers can infer the truth of assertions from natural-language facts and rules generated from a controlled theory, with theorem-prover-derived labels and explicit reasoning-depth splits. The reported models reached about 99% accuracy on standard settings, above 95% on substantially deeper chains than seen during training, and transferred to hand-authored and paraphrased rulebases. Its limitations are the synthetic grammar, restricted vocabulary, and narrow rule language; it tests rule chaining rather than categorical syllogistic moods, open-ended argument interpretation, or rich proof quality. The benchmark is nevertheless a canonical baseline for deductive LLM evaluation because it makes depth, closed-world assumptions, and generalization measurable and establishes the soft-theorem-prover framing. Source: https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/2020/537

paper_heading: Tafjord, Dalvi Mishra & Clark (2021), “ProofWriter: Generating Implications, Proofs, and Abductive Statements over Natural Language”
summary_text: ProofWriter extends RuleTaker-style natural-language theories from classifying preselected claims to generating logical implications, natural-language proofs, and constrained abductive explanations. It evaluates depth-controlled datasets, including unseen-depth and out-of-domain settings, and reports proof accuracy exceeding earlier reconstruction methods by 9 percentage points on RuleTaker while also providing strong baselines for implication enumeration and abduction. The limitation is that the theories remain largely templated and Datalog-like, so exact proof correctness does not test nuanced interpretation of real arguments, quantifier ambiguity, or human content effects. The work is highly relevant to benchmark design because it demonstrates that answer labels, proof certificates, consequence enumeration, and abduction should be treated as distinct evaluation targets rather than collapsed into one accuracy number. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2021.findings-acl.317.pdf

paper_heading: Tian et al. (2021), “Diagnosing the First-Order Logical Reasoning Ability Through LogicNLI”
summary_text: LogicNLI is an NLI-style first-order-logic benchmark built from facts, rules, and hypotheses, covering combinations of core logical operators while minimizing commonsense interference; it adds a “Paradox” relation for cases where both a proposition and its negation can be derived through different paths. BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet are evaluated across accuracy, robustness, generalization, and interpretability/traceability, and the reported models perform above random but below human performance, exposing weaknesses in FOL reasoning. Its limitation is the controlled logical language and pre-generative-LLM model regime, with no direct coverage of classical syllogistic figure or belief-bias effects. Its relevance is the diagnostic separation of entailment, contradiction, neutral, and inconsistency-like cases, which supports richer labels and robustness tests in a new deductive benchmark. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.303/

paper_heading: Han et al. (2022/2024), “FOLIO: Natural Language Reasoning with First-Order Logic”
summary_text: FOLIO evaluates deductive validity over human-authored natural-language premise sets and conclusions paired with first-order-logic annotations; its 1,430 unique conclusions are drawn from 487 premise sets, and an inference engine automatically verifies the formal annotations. The dataset supports both natural-language reasoning and NL-to-FOL translation, and the paper reports systematic experiments across multiple language models, including evidence that a difficult subset challenges GPT-4. Its limitations are that conclusion-level validity and translation accuracy still do not fully measure proof structure, minimal premise use, or alternative valid derivations, while formal annotation imposes an intended interpretation on potentially ambiguous language. FOLIO is relevant as a strong naturalness and logical-diversity baseline and as precedent for evaluating parsing/formalization separately from downstream deduction. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00840

paper_heading: Saparov & He (2022), “Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought” (PrOntoQA)
summary_text: PrOntoQA generates question-answering problems from synthetic first-order world models so that a model’s chain of thought can be parsed into symbolic proof steps and analyzed by proof depth. Experiments with GPT-3 and InstructGPT found that models can often execute individual deduction steps correctly, including in fictional settings, but struggle with proof planning when multiple valid next steps must be explored. Its limitation is the restricted ontology and largely repeated modus-ponens-style structure, which makes it a controlled proof-depth test rather than a broad benchmark of categorical syllogisms, natural argumentation, or belief effects. It is relevant because it provides a clean precedent for separating final-answer accuracy from proof validity, search/planning behavior, and chain-of-thought faithfulness. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01240

paper_heading: Srivastava et al. (2022), “Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and Extrapolating the Capabilities of Language Models” (BIG-bench)
summary_text: BIG-bench is a collaborative suite of 204 tasks evaluated across model families and scales, with human-rater baselines and task families covering logical deduction, categorical/formal syllogisms, and logical fallacies. Its results show broad scale-related improvement but generally poor absolute performance and calibration relative to human raters, while some multistep or brittle tasks display non-smooth capability changes. The limitation is that task-level binary or multiple-choice scoring can conflate reasoning with parsing and format compliance, and some tasks do not expose unknown, contradiction, proof, or error-type distinctions. BIG-bench is relevant as an ecosystem-level precedent for standardized zero-/few-shot evaluation and for placing syllogistic validity, formal fallacies, and general logical deduction in a common test suite. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.04615

paper_heading: Sanyal, Singh & Ren (2022), “FaiRR: Faithful and Robust Deductive Reasoning over Natural Language”
summary_text: FaiRR evaluates deductive reasoning over natural-language rulebases by decomposing the task into independently modeled rule selection, fact selection, and knowledge composition components, thereby creating an explicit causal route from selected premises to generated inferences. On existing reasoning datasets, the authors report robustness to novel language perturbations, faster inference than prior approaches, and more interpretable errors than black-box generative proof systems. Its limitation is that the underlying rule-based regime remains controlled and does not directly address categorical quantifier moods, belief bias, premise-order effects, or open-ended argument structure. The work is relevant to benchmark construction because it motivates scoring evidence selection and derivation faithfulness separately from the final label and provides a model-side template for diagnosing whether a failure arose from premise selection or composition. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.77/

paper_heading: Pan et al. (2023), “Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning”
summary_text: Logic-LM evaluates a pipeline in which an LLM translates a natural-language problem into a symbolic representation, a deterministic solver performs inference, and solver feedback drives self-refinement. It is tested on ProofWriter, PrOntoQA, FOLIO, LogicalDeduction, and AR-LSAT, achieving an average improvement of 39.2% over standard prompting and 18.4% over chain-of-thought prompting. Its limitations are dependence on the expressiveness of the selected symbolic solver and on in-context translation/self-refinement, which can fail for intricate or poorly expressible logical grammars; solver success also does not guarantee that the initial formalization captured the intended meaning. Its relevance is as a direct precedent for reporting parser/formalization errors separately from solver errors and for evaluating deductive benchmarks with hybrid symbolic verification. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.248/

paper_heading: Wu et al. (2023), “Hence, Socrates is mortal: A Benchmark for Natural Language Syllogistic Reasoning” (SylloBase)
summary_text: SylloBase is a direct natural-language syllogism benchmark designed to cover a complete taxonomy of syllogistic reasoning patterns and both generation and understanding tasks. It contains 50,000 template-based samples mined from Wikidata and ConceptNet, GPT-3 paraphrases, and 1,000 manually rewritten test examples; T5 obtains a best generation ROUGE-L of 38.72 and RoBERTa a best multiple-choice accuracy of 72.77%. Its limitations are artifact risk from template construction and GPT-3 paraphrasing, plus an emphasis on answer prediction rather than proof generation, minimal-premise use, or invariance under irrelevant premise/order changes. It is highly relevant as an existing baseline against which any new categorical-syllogism benchmark must demonstrate added value beyond taxonomy coverage and surface naturalness. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.148/

paper_heading: Ando et al. (2023), “Evaluating Large Language Models with NeuBAROCO: Syllogistic Reasoning Ability and Human-like Biases”
summary_text: NeuBAROCO repurposes a dataset originally created for psychological experiments into English- and Japanese-language LLM evaluations of categorical syllogisms, including belief bias, conversion errors, and atmosphere effects. The experiments find that current LLMs struggle more on problems involving these human-associated bias conditions, linking model behavior to established cognitive-science phenomena rather than only measuring aggregate validity. Its limitations are the need to disentangle dataset provenance, translation/language effects, and genuine bias resemblance; reproducing a human error pattern is not evidence of logically valid reasoning. The paper is relevant because it establishes multilingual, psychologically grounded bias testing as a benchmark dimension and supports evaluating content effects and indeterminate relations alongside correctness. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2023.naloma-1.1.pdf

paper_heading: Ozeki et al. (2024), “Exploring Reasoning Biases in Large Language Models Through Syllogism: Insights from the NeuBAROCO Dataset”
summary_text: This follow-up NeuBAROCO study evaluates English and Japanese syllogistic problems using entailment, contradiction, and neutral cases, and adds a Translate-and-Explain chain-of-thought procedure that asks models to formalize the syllogism before explaining their reasoning. The results report human-like reasoning biases, additional model-specific error tendencies, and especially poor performance when the relation is neither entailment nor contradiction; analysis suggests that reasoning-process failures are more important than basic syllogism interpretation errors. Its limitation is that it is closely related to the 2023 NeuBAROCO report rather than an independent benchmark family, and the translation-plus-explanation protocol may itself introduce prompt and language artifacts. It is relevant as evidence that neutral/indeterminate cases and separate parsing-versus-reasoning diagnostics are essential for a modern syllogistic benchmark. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04403

paper_heading: Eisape et al. (2023/2024), “A Systematic Comparison of Syllogistic Reasoning in Humans and Language Models”
summary_text: This study compares human behavior with PaLM 2 and related language-model variants on two-premise categorical syllogisms, probing model scale, premise/term ordering, and classic syllogistic fallacies. Larger PaLM 2 models are reported to be more logical than smaller models and, on the studied items, more logical than humans, but even the largest models remain sensitive to irrelevant variable ordering and make confident invalid inferences that resemble human biases. Its limitations are the time-specific model family and prompt protocol, and human-like behavior is not necessarily the target for an LLM benchmark because humans can be systematically wrong. Its relevance is particularly strong for paired invariance and human/model evaluation: it shows that aggregate accuracy must be supplemented with order perturbations, fallacy profiles, calibration, and confidence/error analysis. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00445

paper_heading: Abe et al. (2024/2025), “Abductive Reasoning with Syllogistic Forms in Large Language Models”
summary_text: This paper converts a syllogistic dataset into an abductive task in which models choose which candidate premise best explains an observed conclusion, while also comparing abductive and deductive judgments. The released data encode English premises and hypotheses, gold abductive and deductive labels, syllogistic figure/form and term-order metadata, contradiction labels, and belief-consistency categories; the work frames abduction as a complementary form of reasoning rather than a replacement for deduction. Its limitation is conceptual as well as empirical: explanatory adequacy is not deductive validity, and the publication metadata differ across the Springer/HAR record and the later arXiv version, so bibliography details require care. It is relevant as an adjacent contrast benchmark that can test whether an LLM distinguishes necessary consequence from plausible explanation instead of silently pooling both under “reasoning accuracy.” Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06428

paper_heading: Schwitzgebel, Schwitzgebel & Strasser — “Creating a Large Language Model of a Philosopher” (Mind & Language; 2023/2024)
summary_text: This paper fine-tunes GPT-3 on Daniel Dennett’s writings to test whether an LLM can reproduce a particular philosopher’s intellectual and stylistic profile. Its central evidence is a comparison involving Dennett, the model, and ten philosophical questions, followed by discrimination experiments in which experts and non-experts attempt to distinguish real-Dennett from model-generated answers; the study reports that model answers can be difficult to identify, especially when multiple answers are considered rather than a single cherry-picked example. The main limitations are the narrow single-philosopher setting, dependence on textual imitation, possible contamination or familiarity with Dennett’s published positions, and the fact that indistinguishable prose does not establish understanding, authorship, consciousness, or valid argumentation. For philosophical LLM research, it is the clearest precedent for philosopher-style generation and sets a high bar: new work must add stronger grounding, argument-structure evaluation, longitudinal revision, source faithfulness, or independent expert assessment rather than claiming novelty from fluent philosopher-like text alone. [Source: arXiv 2302.01339](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01339)

paper_heading: Yang et al. — “InterIDEAS: Philosophical Intertextuality via LLMs” (EMNLP 2025)
summary_text: InterIDEAS contributes a dataset and LLM-assisted workflow for studying how ideas circulate through authentic philosophical texts. The authors combine literary theories of intertextuality, bibliometric relations, GPT-4, retrieval-augmented generation, prompt engineering, and iterative expert review; the pipeline chunks and embeds texts, retrieves relevant passages, extracts reference attributes such as content type, intertextual function, and sentiment, and produces a dataset containing 2,236 reference–attitude pairs for downstream evaluation. Evidence includes ablation and human-in-the-loop validation of the extraction workflow, plus demonstrations of quantitative and qualitative analyses of philosophical relations and a sentiment-classification benchmark. Limitations include dependence on prompt design and retrieval quality, the interpretive instability of labels such as sentiment and intertextual function, residual hallucination risk, and the danger that structured extraction simplifies subtle philosophical reasoning. The paper is directly relevant to philosophical generation and evaluation because it establishes prior art for corpus-scale philosophical RAG and intertextual analysis; a new context engine must therefore distinguish itself through argument-form awareness, proof-relevant retrieval, faithfulness tests, or better independent evaluation. [Source: ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1180/)

paper_heading: Millière & Buckner — “A Philosophical Introduction to Language Models—Part I: Continuity With Classic Debates” (2024)
summary_text: Part I is a philosophical survey and technical primer that situates contemporary LLMs within debates about compositionality, language acquisition, semantic competence, grounding, world models, and cultural transmission. Its contribution is argumentative rather than a new benchmark: it uses the capabilities of systems such as GPT-4 to challenge strong assumptions about neural networks while preserving the “Blockhead” or shallow-pattern-matching hypothesis as a skeptical alternative and calling for empirical investigation of internal mechanisms. The evidence is a systematic engagement with classic philosophy of language, cognitive science, AI, and computational-linguistics findings, including the observation that statistical learners can acquire substantial syntactic structure from exposure. Its limitations are those of an opinionated survey: it does not independently settle the competence-versus-performance dispute, and its conclusions depend on contested philosophical background commitments and the state of empirical evidence reviewed. It is essential for philosophical LLM work because it prevents category errors: fluent output, benchmark success, and apparent semantic competence must be separated from grounding, internal representation, and genuine philosophical understanding. [Source: arXiv 2401.03910](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.03910v1)

paper_heading: Millière & Buckner — “A Philosophical Introduction to Language Models—Part II: The Way Forward” (2024)
summary_text: Part II extends the survey toward empirical and methodological questions, covering mechanistic and causal-intervention approaches, multimodal and modular systems, agency, consciousness, cognitive modeling, secrecy, reproducibility, and benchmark validity. Its strongest contribution to evaluation is the warning that benchmark saturation may reflect gamification, contamination, or ill-defined constructs rather than a genuine increase in competence; the paper argues that interventions and interpretability can provide evidence beyond surface behavior. The evidence consists of philosophical analysis tied to emerging empirical methods and case discussions of how internal mechanisms, architecture, and training conditions bear on claims about cognition. Limitations include the survey’s dependence on rapidly changing technical literature and the fact that causal interpretability methods themselves remain incomplete and theory-laden. For philosophical text generation and evaluation, this paper requires explicit construct definitions, contamination controls, robustness to prompt variation, and—where claims concern reasoning or understanding—tests that go beyond answer accuracy or an LLM judge’s impression. [Source: arXiv 2405.03207](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.03207v1)

paper_heading: Oka — “Evaluating Large Language Models on the Frame and Symbol Grounding Problems: A Zero-shot Benchmark” (2025)
summary_text: Oka operationalizes two classical AI-philosophy problems as zero-shot LLM tasks: a frame-problem scenario requiring relevant-information filtering and plan revision in a changing urban environment, and a symbol-grounding task involving a novel object called a “kluben,” whose properties must be integrated into coherent meanings and relations. The study evaluates 13 closed and open models across repeated trials with multiple criteria aimed at contextual reasoning, semantic coherence, information filtering, and consistency; the reported pattern is that leading closed models perform more stably, while many open models vary substantially and symbol-grounding scores often exceed frame-problem scores. Its limitations are substantial: the prompt reformulations may capture only selected behavioral analogues of the philosophical problems, custom criteria may not be fully independent of the author’s theoretical assumptions, and high scores do not demonstrate intrinsic grounding or commonsense cognition. The paper is a direct precedent for philosophical-problem benchmarking, so new work should improve construct validity through preregistered human rubrics, adversarial paraphrases, independent adjudication, contamination checks, and separate measurement of relevance filtering, semantic integration, and philosophical interpretation. [Source: arXiv 2506.07896](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.07896v1)

paper_heading: Li et al. — “I Think, Therefore I am: Benchmarking Awareness of Large Language Models Using AwareBench” (2024)
summary_text: AwareBench introduces a taxonomy and dataset for evaluating purported LLM awareness across five dimensions: capability, mission, emotion, culture, and perspective. AwareEval combines binary, multiple-choice, and open-ended questions generated through a human–AI collaborative process, and the authors evaluate 13 LLMs; the reported evidence shows that most models struggle with capability and mission awareness while performing better on social-interaction-related dimensions. The benchmark’s contribution is to make self-model and social-awareness claims behaviorally testable and to connect them to alignment and safety. Its limitations are conceptual and methodological: “awareness” is defined behaviorally, the question sets partly rely on model-generated material, anthropomorphic interpretations remain possible, and answering self-referential questions cannot establish phenomenal consciousness, stable self-knowledge, or a philosophically substantive subject. It is directly relevant to AI-philosopher projects involving self-reflection or personhood: self-report-like philosophical answers should be treated as outputs to evaluate for calibration, consistency, and capability awareness—not as evidence that the model is conscious or genuinely self-aware. [Source: arXiv 2401.17882](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.17882v2)

paper_heading: Smart, Clowes & Clark — “ChatGPT, extended: large language models and the extended mind” (Synthese, 2025)
summary_text: This paper develops “Digital Andy,” a system that uses retrieval-augmented generation over Andy Clark’s writings to answer questions about the extended mind, and then analyzes the system through the philosophical framework of active externalism and extended cognition. Its contribution is twofold: it presents RAG as an alternative to fine-tuning for incorporating philosophical knowledge and uses the engineering arrangement to ask whether externally retrieved resources can count as part of an extended artificial cognitive system. The evidence is the system design and philosophical comparison between internal model memory, external retrieval, and the conditions under which information becomes functionally available to the agent. Limitations include the gap between an interpretive philosophical proposal and a demonstrated cognitive status, the dependence of the result on how “accessibility,” memory, and agency are operationalized, and the absence of evidence that RAG produces human-like understanding. The paper matters for philosophical context engines because it directly precedes claims about external philosophical memory: retrieval utility and extended-mind status must be evaluated separately, with explicit criteria for causal dependence, accessibility, reliability, and user/system agency. [Source: institutional repository](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/502110)

paper_heading: Galatolo, Rappuoli, Winkle & Beloucif — “Beyond Ethical Alignment: Evaluating LLMs as Artificial Moral Assistants” (2025)
summary_text: This paper formalizes what an Artificial Moral Assistant should do and introduces AMAeval, a benchmark designed to test explicit moral reasoning rather than only agreement with a target ethical verdict. Drawing on philosophical literature, the framework distinguishes deductive and abductive moral reasoning and evaluates open LLMs both on generating and assessing reasoning chains; the reported results show substantial variation across models, persistent weakness in abductive reasoning, and a separation between evaluation and generation abilities. The contribution is therefore a bridge from normative theory to operational evaluation, with moral reasoning treated as structured deliberation involving conflicting values rather than mere alignment. Limitations include dependence on the selected AMA theory, the difficulty of validating generated reasoning chains independently, possible rubric and dataset biases, and the risk that verbalized chains rationalize rather than reveal the causal basis of decisions. It is a key baseline for philosophical moral assistants: any new system should compare against AMAeval and report premise-level validity, abductive adequacy, uncertainty, plural-tradition robustness, and independent human or expert judgments—not just verdict agreement. [Source: arXiv 2508.12754](https://arxiv.org/html/2508.12754v1)

paper_heading: Asghari & Biały — “Triangles, Justice, and AI: Testing Large Language Models’ Comprehension of Political Ideologies” (Philosophy & Digitality, 2025)
summary_text: This study tests whether LLMs can apply Rawlsian and Nozickian theories of justice to a novel thought experiment involving sentient geometric shapes whose number of angles affects political status. Seven models are evaluated at three levels inspired by Bloom’s taxonomy—recall, application, and reflection—so the task distinguishes remembering theory from transferring it to an unfamiliar scenario and critically reflecting on its implications. The evidence shows large variation across models: one system gives sophisticated theory-consistent responses while others produce confused or generic answers, suggesting that some models can map ideological concepts onto novel cases without implying human-like understanding. Limitations include a small theory set, a single stylized scenario, possible sensitivity to prompt wording and model familiarity with Rawls and Nozick, and scoring that may conflate doctrinal fluency with philosophical comprehension. The paper is a direct precedent for evaluating philosophical-theory transfer; future benchmarks should add paraphrased and adversarial scenarios, opposing traditions, counterexamples, cross-theory consistency, premise-level argument analysis, and blinded expert scoring. [Source: Philosophy & Digitality](https://journals.ub.uni-koeln.de/index.php/phidi/article/view/11663)

paper_heading: Chen et al. — “Leveraging large language models to assist philosophical counseling: prospective techniques, value, and challenges” (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 2025)
summary_text: This article surveys prospective uses of prompt engineering, fine-tuning, and RAG in philosophical counseling, including counselor recommendation, pre-counseling assessment, in-session guidance, session summarization, outcome evaluation, and cultural adaptation. Its contribution is an application-oriented account of how LLMs could expand access and reduce administrative burden while insisting that systems should augment rather than replace professional counselors. The evidence is primarily conceptual and illustrative: the article synthesizes counseling requirements, proposes technical workflows, and discusses generated summaries and recommendation functions alongside risks involving hallucination, privacy, explainability, trust, and the lack of genuine understanding or empathy. Its limitations are the absence of controlled counseling-outcome experiments, limited evidence that proposed methods improve philosophical rather than generic conversational support, and the high-stakes difficulty of mental-health triage and personalized advice. It is relevant to philosophical dialogue generation because it shows that useful assistance, safe deployment, and legitimate philosophical agency are distinct claims; a new assistant needs bounded tasks, human oversight, privacy protections, factual and interpretive faithfulness tests, and failure analysis rather than a generic chatbot demonstration. [Source: Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-025-04657-7)

paper_heading: Millière & Buckner — “The Philosophy of Language Models” (Philosophy Compass, 2026)
summary_text: This broad survey synthesizes philosophical disagreements about LLMs across syntactic competence, compositionality, meaning, representation, attitudes, reasoning, agency, and consciousness. Its central contribution is methodological: it argues that progress requires both explicit philosophical commitments and close engagement with empirical evidence, including interpretability and causal evidence where behavioral performance underdetermines the underlying mechanism. The article’s evidence is a structured review of classic arguments and contemporary empirical work, framed around the conflict between human-like-capacity interpretations and shallow pattern-matching interpretations. As a survey, it does not provide a new experimental adjudication, and its conclusions remain sensitive to unresolved disputes over what counts as meaning, reasoning, agency, or consciousness. For philosophical LLM generation and evaluation, it is the most current high-level warning against unqualified claims: research should maintain separate evidence tracks for output quality, doctrinal or argumentative competence, internal representation, causal mechanism, and philosophical status, and should state clearly which track its results support. [Source: Philosophy Compass/Wiley](https://compass.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/phc3.70095)

paper_heading: Abdali et al. — “Self-reflecting Large Language Models: A Hegelian Dialectical Approach” (2025; arXiv version updated 2026)
summary_text:
This paper builds a self-reflection framework around a Hegelian dialectical pattern: an initial proposition is challenged by an opposition and reconciled through a more comprehensive synthesis. It applies the iterative procedure to scientific-idea generation and error correction, compares dynamic temperature annealing with constant temperature, and introduces Multi-Agent Majority Voting (MAMV) so multiple LLMs assess validity and novelty when domain experts are unavailable; the paper reports gains over baselines on GSM8K, GSM-hard, GSM-Symbolic, and MMLU Pro, with qualitative results for open-ended ideation. Its limitations are especially important for philosophical evaluation: the Hegelian terminology may function mainly as prompt scaffolding rather than an operational account of dialectic, MAMV is circular when LLMs judge LLM-generated ideas, and model agreement is a weak proxy for validity, novelty, or philosophical insight. The paper is direct precedent for dialectical prompting, multi-agent critique, and philosophical idea generation; a stronger system should use independently authored rubrics, expert adjudication on a frozen subset, source and argument verification, and novelty tests that do not rely solely on LLM consensus. [Source: arXiv 2501.14917](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14917)

## Cross-paper implication

Across the 12 papers, the literature already covers philosopher-style imitation, philosophical-text RAG and intertextuality, classical AI-philosophy benchmarks, awareness probes, extended-mind interpretations, moral reasoning, political-theory transfer, philosophical counseling, and dialectical self-critique. The defensible remaining gap is narrower: an argument-form-aware philosophical context engine that identifies premises, conclusions, inference type, source tradition, and uncertainty; retrieves or compresses proof-relevant passages; and evaluates generated outputs with independent philosophical rubrics, contamination controls, faithfulness measures, and human/expert validation rather than style, verdict agreement, or circular LLM judging alone.

paper_heading: Gao et al. (2023), “Comparing scientific abstracts generated by ChatGPT to real abstracts with detectors and blinded human reviewers”
summary_text: Gao et al. generated 50 medical abstracts from article titles and journal identities using an early ChatGPT version, then compared them with the originals using plagiarism/similarity tools, the GPT-2 Output Detector, journal-format checks, and blinded human reviewers. The generated texts were superficially formatted as scientific abstracts, but only 8/50 correctly followed the target journal’s heading/structure conventions; the detector achieved AUROC 0.94, reviewers correctly identified 68% of generated abstracts, and incorrectly labeled 14% of original abstracts as AI-generated. The design tests plausibility and provenance detection rather than scientific truth, because the model did not receive the underlying articles, methods, or data, and the corpus and model were from late 2022/early 2023. For this project, the paper supports separating fluency, format compliance, factuality, and authorship detection into distinct evaluation dimensions rather than treating detectability or surface quality as evidence of research quality. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-023-00819-6)

paper_heading: Herbold et al. (2023), “A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays”
summary_text: Herbold et al. compared a large corpus of human argumentative student essays with essays generated by ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 from matched prompts, using teacher ratings on standard quality criteria and computational linguistic analysis of logical structure, language complexity, vocabulary richness, and linking. The AI essays received higher average quality ratings, with GPT-4 outperforming GPT-3.5 and humans on several structural and linguistic dimensions; the models also showed recognizable regularities such as formulaic conclusions, more nominalizations, and fewer discourse/epistemic markers. The study concerns student essays rather than evidence-heavy scholarly research, and its prompts were generally not designed to test citation accuracy, empirical validity, or original research reasoning, so the result cannot be generalized to reliable academic scholarship. It is directly useful here as a decomposition of writing quality into argument structure, topical coverage, language, complexity, vocabulary, and cohesion, while demonstrating why those dimensions must be scored separately from truth and evidential support. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-45644-9)

paper_heading: Yeadon et al. (2024), “Evaluating AI and human authorship quality in academic writing through physics essays”
summary_text: Yeadon et al. evaluated 300 short physics-essay submissions, equally divided between pre-ChatGPT student work and GPT-4 outputs, within a course covering history and philosophy of physics, science communication, and ethics in academia; five independent markers graded blinded essay sets and then judged likely authorship, while five commercial detectors were also compared. Human and AI essays did not differ significantly in grades (p = 0.107), markers were only marginally better than chance at authorship identification, and ZeroGPT performed best in the study’s binary detector comparison, reporting 98% accuracy under that specific setup. The sample came from one module, used short essays and one model/version, and detector results are corpus-dependent; the detector headline should not be treated as evidence of general authorship reliability. The study is valuable for this project because it cleanly separates academic-writing quality from provenance classification and provides a philosophy-adjacent test context in which content quality, reasoning, and authorship should be evaluated as different endpoints. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6404/ad669d)

paper_heading: Kong and Liu (2024), “A comparative genre analysis of AI-generated and scholar-written abstracts for English review articles in international journals”
summary_text: Kong and Liu constructed two corpora of 160 scholar-written and 160 ChatGPT-generated review-article abstracts spanning four hard- and soft-science disciplines, then compared their rhetorical moves, move order, obligatory and optional elements, and move embedding. They found significant differences in the frequency of three of five rhetorical moves, preferred sequencing, and embedding frequency, although the two groups shared some embedding combinations and broad structural patterns. The evaluation is about genre realization and disciplinary organization, not whether the abstracts’ claims are true, whether evidence supports them, or whether the underlying reviews are novel or methodologically sound; it also uses abstracts rather than full papers. For this project, the paper offers an operational alternative to vague judgments that text “sounds academic”: disciplinary genre knowledge, rhetorical-move coverage, ordering, and embedding can be scored separately from grammar, readability, factuality, and argument validity. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeap.2024.101432)

paper_heading: Geng and Trotta (2024), “Is ChatGPT Transforming Academics’ Writing Style?”
summary_text: Geng and Trotta analyzed approximately one million arXiv abstracts submitted from May 2018 through January 2024 and calibrated a statistical style model using real abstracts and simulated ChatGPT-modified abstracts produced with a simple “revise the following sentences” prompt. They estimated increasing ChatGPT-like stylistic influence, especially in computer science, with roughly 35% of abstracts classified as exhibiting the modeled style under their baseline assumptions. The estimate measures resemblance to a simulated style distribution, not actual ChatGPT use, authorship, factuality, quality, or research merit; it is also sensitive to prompt choice, calibration data, field differences, and temporal shifts in academic language. This paper matters for the project as a warning that human/AI comparisons and detector performance may drift as people adopt model-like phrasing, making style-based provenance a moving target rather than a stable proxy for authorship or scholarly quality. (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.08627)

paper_heading: Thelwall (2024), “Can ChatGPT evaluate research quality?”
summary_text: Thelwall configured GPT-4 to apply UK Research Excellence Framework-style criteria for significance, rigor, and originality to 51 of the author’s own journal articles, repeating the evaluation 15 times and comparing the outputs with the author’s self-evaluations. Single-run scores correlated weakly with the self-ratings (mean r = 0.281), while averaging repeated runs improved the correlation to 0.509; after removing the weakest articles, the average-score correlation fell to r = 0.200 and was no longer statistically significant, indicating difficulty with fine-grained judgments. The study uses a convenience sample from one author and one field, relies on self-evaluation rather than independent expert consensus, and is prompt/model dependent, so it is not a general validation of LLM peer review. It directly supports this project’s requirement to test evaluator stability, calibration, human agreement, and criterion-level validity rather than accepting plausible rationales or one-shot scores as evidence that an AI judge can assess philosophical or academic research quality. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.2478/jdis-2024-0013)

paper_heading: Levin et al. (2024), “Association of reviewer experience with discriminating human-written versus ChatGPT-written abstracts”
summary_text: Levin et al. created 10 fabricated gynecologic-oncology abstracts and matched ChatGPT-3.5 abstracts from the same titles and results, then asked 30 reviewers—10 residents, 10 junior reviewers, and 10 senior reviewers—to classify 20 blinded abstracts, yielding 600 judgments. Reviewers correctly classified 50% overall, including only 46.3% of ChatGPT abstracts; seniority, publication experience, and AI familiarity were associated with better identification, while human-written abstracts were identified more accurately than generated ones. Because both sets were fabricated and matched, the study tests provenance discrimination rather than medical correctness, clinical usefulness, or research quality; its small, domain-specific sample also limits generalization. For this project, it shows that evaluator expertise can affect authorship judgments and should be recorded, but that even experienced reviewers’ ability to identify AI text does not establish that they can assess argument validity, factuality, or scholarly contribution. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1136/ijgc-2023-005162)

paper_heading: Bohlmann and Berger (2024), “ChatGPT and the Writing of Philosophical Essays: An Experimental Study with Prospective Teachers on How the Turing Test Inverted”
summary_text: Bohlmann and Berger conducted a philosophy-specific experiment in which prospective teachers judged philosophical essays written by students and by ChatGPT, comparing human discrimination performance with an AI classifier. The indexed scholarly record reports approximately 78.7% classification accuracy, making the study unusually direct evidence about whether philosophical prose can be identified by its provenance. The available record exposes less methodological detail than the full methods needed for assessing philosophical competence, and authorship classification is not the same as evaluating interpretation, premise quality, validity, counterargument handling, or originality; the result therefore should not be read as a measure of philosophical writing quality. Its main value for this project is domain specificity: philosophy requires a separate evaluation layer for reasoning and textual engagement even when a classifier or reader can distinguish likely AI authorship. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.5840/teachphil202451200)

paper_heading: Schwitzgebel, Schwitzgebel, and Strasser (2023/2024), “Creating a Large Language Model of a Philosopher”
summary_text: Schwitzgebel and collaborators fine-tuned GPT-3 on Daniel Dennett’s writings, asked Dennett and the model the same 10 philosophical questions, collected four model responses per question without cherry-picking, and recruited 425 participants consisting of Dennett experts, philosophy-blog readers, and ordinary participants to identify the human philosopher’s answer. Experts achieved 51% accuracy against a 20% chance baseline, philosophy-blog readers performed similarly, and ordinary participants were near chance; for two questions, an AI response was selected more often than Dennett’s actual answer. The task is short-response style and voice imitation, not full academic papers, source-grounded exegesis, valid argument construction, or research originality, and the arXiv version should be distinguished from the later journal publication. For this project, it demonstrates that convincing philosophical voice and human-like reception are independent of argument validity, factuality, attribution, and scholarly accountability, reinforcing the need for construct-specific evaluation. (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01339)

paper_heading: Alkaissi and McFarlane (2023), “Artificial Hallucinations in ChatGPT: Implications in Scientific Writing”
summary_text: Alkaissi and McFarlane used prompted short paragraphs on medical and non-medical topics as an editorial case study of ChatGPT’s scientific-writing behavior, checking whether fluent outputs contained plausible but incorrect claims and references. They report that the model could produce convincing prose while mixing accurate material with fabricated or erroneous facts and citations, illustrating how apparent expertise can conceal unsupported content. This is not a systematic benchmark: the prompt set is small, the design is editorial rather than independently rated, and it does not estimate hallucination rates across models, domains, or prompt conditions. For this project, the paper supplies a foundational factuality warning and motivates explicit claim-level checks for source existence, bibliographic correctness, entailment, uncertainty, and evidence support instead of using coherence or style as a proxy for truth. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.35179)

paper_heading: Bhattacharyya et al. (2023), “High Rates of Fabricated and Inaccurate References in ChatGPT-Generated Medical Content”
summary_text: Bhattacharyya et al. prompted ChatGPT-3.5 to generate 30 short medical papers with at least three references each, then verified reference authenticity and the accuracy of seven bibliographic elements using Medline, Google Scholar, and the Directory of Open Access Journals. Of 115 generated references, 47% were fabricated, 46% were authentic but inaccurate, and only 7% were both authentic and accurate; incorrect PMID, volume, page, and year fields were common, with an average of 4.3 inaccurate elements per reference. The study is limited to early ChatGPT-3.5, medical prompts, and short generated papers, so rates should not be transferred directly to philosophy or current models, and it evaluates references rather than complete argument quality. It directly supports a paper-level reference audit in this project covering existence, metadata match, relevance, and whether each citation actually supports the claim for which it is supplied. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.7759/cureus.39238)

paper_heading: Ide, Nakagawa, and collaborators (2023), “Can ChatGPT Be Considered an Author of a Medical Article?”
summary_text: Ide et al. applied the four International Committee of Medical Journal Editors authorship criteria to ChatGPT, distinguishing contribution to conception/design or analysis, drafting/revision, final approval, and accountability for accuracy and integrity. Their analysis concluded that ChatGPT can assist with contribution and drafting but cannot give final approval or accept responsibility for the article, so it should not be listed as an author under ICMJE criteria even though its use should be disclosed. This is a normative/accountability analysis rather than an empirical test of generated prose, scientific validity, or model behavior across tasks, and its conclusion is tied to a particular medical-publishing framework. For this project, it provides a useful multidimensional authorship taxonomy: generation assistance, intellectual contribution, approval, attribution, and responsibility should not be collapsed into a single “AI-authored” label. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.2188/jea.JE20230030)

paper_heading: Aylsworth and Castro (2024), “Should I Use ChatGPT to Write My Papers?”
summary_text:
Aylsworth and Castro present a philosophical normative analysis of whether students should use chatbots to write humanities papers, examining competing arguments about cheating, education, capacity loss, agency, and technological assistance before defending a Kantian account centered on the duty to cultivate and safeguard one’s autonomy. Their conclusion is that students have moral reasons to write certain humanities papers themselves because the writing process cultivates the capacity to set and pursue one’s own ends, while permissible assistance may remain available for less educationally central tasks. The paper does not empirically measure ChatGPT’s quality, factuality, reasoning, or student behavior, and its claims depend on a normative account of education and autonomy rather than experimental results. It is nevertheless important to this project because it defines a target construct that technical metrics can miss: a text may be fluent, accurate, and logically organized yet fail an assignment’s agency, authorship, or educational-purpose requirements. (DOI: https://doi.org/10.1007/s13347-024-00809-w)

## Verification note

All 13 retained records were checked against a publisher, repository, PubMed/PMC, arXiv, or institutional scholarly record. The verification also corrected the source attribution for the reference-integrity study: the paper listed in the input inventory as “Sadasivan et al.” is published as Bhattacharyya, Miller, Bhattacharyya, and Miller (2023), DOI 10.7759/cureus.39238. The set contains empirical evaluations, style/provenance studies, a citation-integrity study, an authorship-accountability analysis, and normative philosophy; these constructs should not be pooled into one undifferentiated quality score.

paper_heading: Hong et al. (2022), “Scholastic: Graphical Human-Al Collaboration for Inductive and Interpretive Text Analysis”
summary_text: Hong et al. present *Scholastic*, a human–AI text-analysis interface that combines machine-in-the-loop clustering with researcher-applied codes, structured metadata, hierarchical document and word clusters, and interactive visualizations for inductive and interpretive analysis.[1] The paper is an important verification of a likely false positive: “Scholastic” is the name of an HCI/ML system, not a reference to medieval scholastic method, and the system does not represent a *quaestio*, objections, distinctions, a *respondeo*, or replies. Its exact relevance is consequently low, although it offers a useful precedent for human-guided construction of structured context over a text corpus rather than treating documents as undifferentiated input.[1]

paper_heading: Freedman et al. (2025), “Argumentative Large Language Models for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification”
summary_text: Freedman et al. develop Argumentative Large Language Models (ArgLLMs), which augment language models with an explicit argumentation layer for explainable and contestable claim verification.[2][11] The system constructs argumentation frameworks and applies formal reasoning to evaluate claims, making contestability and explanation first-class properties rather than relying only on an unstructured generated answer. This is a strong adjacent precedent for a scholastic-AI project because objections can be treated as contesting reasons that must be represented and answered; however, the paper does not implement the ordered medieval workflow of question, objection list, distinctions, determination, and targeted replies, nor does it define a scholastic *respondeo* stage.[2][11]

paper_heading: Castagna, Sassoon, and Parsons (2024), “Can formal argumentative reasoning enhance LLMs performances?”
summary_text: Castagna, Sassoon, and Parsons introduce MQArgEng, a proof-of-concept pipeline that inserts computational-argumentation semantics as an argumentation-engine plug-in for an LLM.[3] The reported preliminary MT-Bench experiments indicate moderate gains across most topical categories, supporting the premise that an external formal argument layer can improve LLM reasoning or conversation without retraining the base model. The paper is therefore a high-value comparator for compact philosophical context built around explicit argument relations, but its argumentation engine remains generic: it does not encode scholastic objections, distinctions, authorities, determination, or an ordered reply structure, and it should not be treated as a direct implementation of the scholastic method.[3]

paper_heading: Sanayei et al. (2025), “Can LLMs Judge Debates? Evaluating Non-Linear Reasoning via Argumentation Theory Semantics”
summary_text: Sanayei et al. test whether LLMs can approximate Computational Argumentation Theory semantics when judging dialogue-formatted debates.[4] Using QuAD-style argumentative structures, the study asks models to rank or assess arguments without directly receiving the underlying graph and finds that performance worsens as inputs become longer or discourse flow is disrupted, while stronger prompting can partly reduce positional and length biases. Its direct contribution to a scholastic-AI design is methodological: it shows why extracting a compact argument graph or other explicit structure may be preferable to asking an LLM to recover non-linear relations from a long debate transcript. The work evaluates argument acceptability and ranking, not scholastic determination or the ordered resolution of objections.[4]

paper_heading: Alfano et al. (2026), “LLM-based Argument Mining meets Argumentation and Description Logics: a Unified Framework for Reasoning about Debates”
summary_text: Alfano et al. propose a unified pipeline that uses LLM-assisted argument mining to turn raw debate text into a fuzzy argumentative knowledge base, representing arguments as entities with support or attack relations and initial strengths, applying quantitative argumentation semantics, and embedding the resulting structures into fuzzy description logic for query answering.[5] The full framework separates tasks such as argument tagging, entity extraction, quantitative bipolar argumentation framework extraction, and fuzzy argument-box construction, making it the closest recent technical comparator in this set for span classification, explicit relational context, formal propagation, and queryable reasoning. Its novelty threat is nevertheless adjacent rather than direct: the framework models debates and formal support/attack networks, not the scholastic *quaestio*, enumerated objections, distinctions, determination, or reply ordering.[5]

paper_heading: Mitsuda, Higashinaka, and Saito (2022), “Combining Argumentation Structure and Language Model for Generating Natural Argumentative Dialogue”
summary_text: Mitsuda, Higashinaka, and Saito combine a hand-crafted argumentation structure with a language model that rewrites propositions—using keywords and stance information—into the next natural-language utterance while preserving argumentative context.[6] Their manual evaluation reports improved naturalness without loss of argumentation consistency, establishing a clear separation between a structured argumentative skeleton and surface-language realization. That separation parallels a scholastic-AI architecture in which a system first extracts or constructs a deductive/disputational skeleton and only then generates polished philosophical prose. The paper remains an adjacent dialogue-generation precedent: it does not model objections, distinctions, determination, or scholastic replies as explicit protocol stages.[6]

paper_heading: Sazid et al. (2022), “A Unified Representation and a Decoupled Deep Learning Architecture for Argumentation Mining of Students’ Persuasive Essays”
summary_text: Sazid et al. propose a unified representation and decoupled deep-learning architecture for identifying non-argumentative units, premises, claims, major claims, and relations such as support, attack, for, and against in students’ persuasive essays.[7] The paper is relevant because it demonstrates how text spans can be assigned argument roles and converted into a compact relational representation rather than being processed as undifferentiated prose. That capability could support extraction of premises, claims, and counter-considerations from scholastic texts, but the source domain is monologic essay argument mining: it has no dialogue moves, explicit objection/reply pairs, distinction phase, authority handling, or scholastic resolution stage. It is therefore a medium-strength structural precedent rather than a direct novelty threat.[7]

paper_heading: Macagno (2021), “Argumentation Schemes in AI: A Literature Review. Introduction to the Special Issue”
summary_text: Macagno reviews AI research using Walton-style argumentation schemes and characterizes schemes as dialectical instruments with premises, conclusions, and critical questions.[8] The review explains how critical questions can challenge a scheme’s applicability or shift the burden of proof back to a proponent, and it surveys applications spanning argument mining, representation, multi-agent systems, law, policy, healthcare, economics, and education. This is the strongest conceptual bridge in the set between scholastic-style dialectical organization and computational implementation: critical questions, defeasible presumptions, burden shifting, nested arguments, and dialogue protocols function as partial computational analogues of objections and replies. The limitation is decisive for novelty: the article is a literature review of argumentation schemes, not an LLM system and not a full implementation of the medieval *quaestio/disputatio* sequence.[8]

paper_heading: Walton (2016), “Some Artificial Intelligence Tools for Argument Evaluation: An Introduction”
summary_text: Walton surveys AI tools for evaluating defeasible arguments in legal and everyday conversational settings, emphasizing approaches that go beyond deductive logic and Bayesian rules through argument graphs, argumentation schemes, and systems such as Carneades.[9] The paper supplies foundational prior art for using an intermediate argument representation between natural-language discourse and formal evaluation, which is directly relevant to extracting and checking the reasoning skeleton of scholastic texts. It predates current LLMs and does not address automatic extraction of scholastic components, medieval textual organization, or an explicit question–objection–determination–reply protocol. Its relevance is thus foundational and conceptual rather than a direct system-level overlap.[9]

paper_heading: Shi et al. (2026), “Tackling the Root of Misinformation by Teaching Laypeople about Logical Fallacies via Socratic Questioning and Critical Argumentation”
summary_text:
Shi et al. introduce LFTutor, an LLM-based tutoring system that combines intent-driven Socratic questioning with critical argumentation to teach users to identify logical fallacies.[10] The study reports automatic and human-evaluation gains over baseline LLMs that lack the pedagogical strategies, showing that question-driven challenge and reflective response can be operationalized as a controlled interaction pattern. This is relevant to a scholastic-AI project as a nearby design precedent for generating objections, eliciting commitments, and prompting replies instead of producing a single unsupported answer. Its method is Socratic pedagogy rather than medieval scholastic disputation, and the opened record does not define a *quaestio*, formal objection list, distinction stage, *respondeo*, or determination data structure.[10]

## Synthesis

Across all ten verified papers, the direct duplicate risk remains low: none operationalizes the complete medieval scholastic sequence as an AI/LLM reasoning architecture. The high-risk adjacent convergence is clear, however. Existing work already covers explicit argument representations, support/attack relations, formal argumentation semantics, contestability, debate judging, argument mining, structured dialogue generation, and question-driven critical reasoning. A defensible novelty claim should therefore center on making the scholastic sequence itself a first-class computational object: identify and normalize the question, enumerate objections, distinguish senses or cases, locate authorities and reasons, produce a determination, and attach targeted replies to each objection with provenance.
