paper_heading: Maliszewski, “It takes a village to write a book: Mapping anonymous contributions in Stephen Langton’s *Quaestiones Theologiae” (2025)
summary_text: Maliszewski presents a proposed computational study of Stephen Langton’s *Quaestiones Theologiae*, a collection derived from reportationes of oral teaching, to investigate editorial layers and anonymous contributions. The workflow combines transformer-based handwritten-text recognition and transcription alignment with stylometric features such as frequent words, part-of-speech patterns, and pseudo-affixes, and it explicitly compares manually composed material with automatically extracted transcriptions. Its scholarly target is authorship attribution and reconstruction of the collection’s formation, not the recovery or validation of scholastic inferences; HTR and stylometry operate as evidence about textual production below the level of argument reasoning. The paper is therefore a direct precedent for computational analysis of a scholastic reportatio corpus, while remaining a study design whose results depend on transcription quality, corpus size, and the instability of stylometric signals in short questions. Verified record: [arXiv:2508.12830](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12830); publisher DOI listed in the source record: [10.1017/chr.2025.10004](https://doi.org/10.1017/chr.2025.10004).

paper_heading: Clérice, Vlachou-Efstathiou, and Chagué, “CREMMA Medii Aevi: Literary Manuscript Text Recognition in Latin” (2023)
summary_text: CREMMA Medii Aevi contributes a segmentation and handwritten-text-recognition dataset for Medieval Latin literary manuscripts dating from the eleventh through the sixteenth centuries. The paper adds approximately 263,000 characters under guidelines designed to interoperate with earlier Latin and Medieval French HTR resources, with particular attention to abbreviations, and reports models that improve recognition on unknown Latin manuscripts. This is corpus digitization and AI-assisted transcription: the models make manuscript text more accessible, but they do not normalize the text, identify scholastic genre structure, reconstruct a quaestio, or reason over an argument. Its relevance to scholastic studies is infrastructural, since manuscript witnesses can become machine-readable inputs for later linguistic, transmission, or argument-level work; the dataset itself is broader than scholastic disputations. Verified records: [DOI 10.5334/johd.97](https://doi.org/10.5334/johd.97); [article PDF](https://malamatenia.github.io/pdfs/cremma-medii-aevi.pdf); [Zenodo dataset record](https://zenodo.org/records/7510411).

paper_heading: Koch et al., “A Tailored Handwritten-Text-Recognition System for Medieval Latin” (2023)
summary_text: Koch and colleagues build an end-to-end HTR pipeline for handwritten lemma entries on the Bavarian Medieval Latin Dictionary’s record cards. The system uses image-segmentation models to locate relevant regions and transformer-based vision-encoder/GPT-2-decoder combinations to transcribe them, with extensive data augmentation; the reported best setup achieves a character error rate of 0.015 and is compared with Google Cloud Vision. The contribution is clearly AI transcription for a low-resource historical language rather than AI reasoning: it extracts lexical evidence from images but does not interpret scholastic propositions, represent disputational roles, or test inferences. Because the source material consists of dictionary cards rather than quaestiones or commentaries, its direct relevance is methodological—showing how domain-specific HTR can precede downstream Medieval Latin analysis—and it does not constitute a scholastic argument resource. Verified record: [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/2023.alp-1.12/); [paper PDF](https://aclanthology.org/2023.alp-1.12.pdf); [arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.09368).

paper_heading: McGillivray, Passarotti, and Ruffolo, “The Index Thomisticus Treebank Project: Annotation, Parsing and Valency Lexicon” (2009)
summary_text: This paper introduces the Index Thomisticus Treebank as a dependency-annotated resource for Medieval Latin texts by Thomas Aquinas and describes its annotation, parsing experiments, and valency lexicon. The project turns a large Thomistic corpus into machine-readable morphosyntactic structures that support supervised parsing and lexical investigation. It is corpus infrastructure and NLP parsing, not AI reasoning: dependency trees identify syntactic relations and valency patterns, but they do not distinguish objections, authorities, *sed contra*, *respondeo*, replies, or the inferential warrants of a scholastic disputation. The treebank is nevertheless a foundational resource for computational work on Aquinas, including texts adjacent to *Sentences* commentary and disputed-question traditions, and it establishes that the relevant bottleneck is not merely access to Latin text but the addition of genre-aware and argument-level annotation. The source file’s author attribution should be corrected: the ACL record lists Barbara McGillivray, Marco Passarotti, and Paolo Ruffolo. Verified record: [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/2009.tal-2.5/).

paper_heading: Cecchini, Passarotti, Marongiu, and Zeman, “Challenges in Converting the Index Thomisticus Treebank into Universal Dependencies” (2018)
summary_text: This paper revises the conversion of the Index Thomisticus Treebank into Universal Dependencies by harmonizing part-of-speech tags, lemmatization, and dependency relations with other Latin treebanks while correcting errors and inconsistencies in the earlier conversion. The authors evaluate the revised process against a manually checked gold standard and report improved conversion quality, especially for labeled attachment. The work concerns annotation normalization and interoperability, not reasoning: UD makes scholastic Latin accessible to broader NLP tools, but a standardized dependency representation is not a historically neutral account of medieval semantics and does not encode the architecture of a *quaestio* or assess argument validity. Its importance is methodological because it demonstrates that even apparently basic preprocessing decisions can materially affect downstream comparisons, retrieval, and parsing. Verified record: [ACL Anthology](https://aclanthology.org/W18-6004/); [paper PDF](https://aclanthology.org/W18-6004.pdf); [Zenodo repository record](https://zenodo.org/records/2552203).

paper_heading: Gamba, Passarotti, and Ruffolo, “More Data and New Tools: Advances in Parsing the Index Thomisticus Treebank” (2021)
summary_text: Gamba, Passarotti, and Ruffolo evaluate how larger training data and newer parser combinations affect automatic dependency parsing of the Index Thomisticus Treebank. The experiments compare configurations including DeSR and neural parsers and examine ensemble behavior on Medieval Latin Aquinas data, showing that parser performance depends on language-specific modeling and that different systems reproduce characteristic errors. This is supervised AI/NLP at the syntactic level, not reasoning over scholastic arguments: improved attachment scores do not show that a model has reconstructed premises, objections, authorities, replies, or inferential force. The paper is useful as a benchmark precedent because it tests modern parsing assumptions against a historically and linguistically distinctive corpus, while leaving open the much harder problem of connecting parses to disputational structure and historically adequate argument interpretation. Verified record: [CEUR-WS paper PDF](https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-2989/long_paper20.pdf); [Zenodo DOI record](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5599095).

paper_heading: Mambrini, Passarotti, Moretti, and Pellegrini, “The Index Thomisticus Treebank as Linked Data in the LiLa Knowledge Base” (2022)
summary_text: This LREC paper publishes annotation layers from the Index Thomisticus Treebank as Linguistic Linked Open Data within the LiLa Knowledge Base, linking Medieval Latin corpus tokens and dependency structures to interoperable lexical resources. The contribution is knowledge representation and corpus interoperability: persistent identifiers and explicit links make it possible to query text, morphology, syntax, and lexical information across resources. That infrastructure should not be mistaken for an argument graph or reasoning engine, because linked tokens and lexical relations do not by themselves encode premises, conclusions, objection/reply roles, or validity conditions. The work matters for scholastic AI because provenance-preserving links are a prerequisite for assembling contexts that retain the connection between a model’s input and its textual, lexical, and annotation sources. The source file’s author list should be corrected to the LREC record: Francesco Mambrini, Marco Passarotti, Giovanni Moretti, and Matteo Pellegrini. Verified record: [institutional publication record](https://publicatt.unicatt.it/handle/10807/210702); [LREC PDF](https://www.lrec-conf.org/proceedings/lrec2022/pdf/2022.lrec-1.428.pdf).

paper_heading: Nowak, Ziębura, Wróbel, and Smywiński-Pohl, “eFontes: Part of Speech Tagging and Lemmatization of Medieval Latin Texts: A Cross-Genre Survey” (2024)
summary_text: The eFontes study develops transformer-based models for Medieval Latin lemmatization, part-of-speech tagging, and morphological-feature prediction using Universal Dependencies resources and a newly developed corpus of Polish Medieval Latin. It evaluates performance across genres and addresses orthographic variation and Latinized vernacular vocabulary, reporting strong but task-specific accuracy. This is AI/NLP annotation rather than reasoning: the models assign linguistic labels to tokens and do not infer the interpretation or argumentative role of a passage in a scholastic question. The paper is relevant because variation in spelling, vocabulary, and genre can propagate errors into search, quotation alignment, semantic modeling, and any later attempt at argument mining. Its results support treating linguistic annotation as an uncertainty-bearing layer rather than as a transparent substitute for historical reading. Verified record: [arXiv:2407.00418](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00418).

paper_heading: *Corpus Thomisticum* official research infrastructure
summary_text: The *Corpus Thomisticum* is a long-standing digital research infrastructure providing searchable editions of Aquinas’s works, bibliography, research tools, manuscript material, and database functions for words, phrases, quotations, similarities, correlations, and statistics. It is a corpus and retrieval platform rather than a scholarly paper or AI-reasoning system: its search and concordance capabilities enable discovery and comparison, but they do not perform argument-aware retrieval, reconstruct disputational roles, or validate the reasoning of a passage. For scholastic computational research, its significance is foundational because it supplies broad access to Latin texts and manuscript-oriented materials, while also making clear that searchable text is only the first layer of a reasoning-oriented pipeline. Any downstream model must still distinguish editions, witnesses, editorial choices, and passage-level evidence. Verified record: [official introduction](https://corpusthomisticum.org/wintroen.html).

paper_heading: Rockwell and Passarotti, “The Index Thomisticus as a Digital Humanities Big Data Project” (2019)
summary_text: Rockwell and Passarotti analyze the Index Thomisticus as a major Digital Humanities infrastructure project, emphasizing its history, scale, data representation, concordance functions, and the project-management and media-archaeological conditions that made large-scale computational work on Aquinas possible. The paper is a history and analysis of digital infrastructure, not an AI model and not a formal account of scholastic reasoning. Its principal contribution to the present topic is to prevent anachronism: computational engagement with Aquinas predates current machine learning and demonstrates that digitization, indexing, and corpus-scale retrieval have their own long history. The article therefore weakens any novelty claim framed as simply “using computation on Aquinas” and redirects novelty toward provenance-preserving, genre-aware argument representation or evaluation. Verified record: [DOI 10.6092/issn.2532-8816/8575](https://doi.org/10.6092/issn.2532-8816/8575); [open article PDF](https://umanisticadigitale.unibo.it/article/download/8575/9248).

paper_heading: ERC-DEBATE, “Debate: Innovation as Performance in Late-Medieval Universities”
summary_text: The ERC-DEBATE project studies late-medieval university *principia* as public academic performances and builds a corpus-oriented research program around authorship, transmission, neglected texts, and the intellectual dynamics of debate. The project’s CORDIS reporting describes *principia* as structured events combining oral performance, argument, authority, competition, and institutional setting, while the project corpus page frames the recovery and organization of texts across university contexts. This is corpus construction, digital editing, and manuscript/transmission research, not an evaluated AI-reasoning benchmark: identifying or attributing debate texts is different from extracting premises, modeling historically specific argumentative moves, or checking validity. Its importance is that it supplies a debate-centered corpus domain in which future argument-level annotation could be meaningful and provenance-sensitive. Verified records: [DEBATE project site](https://debate-erc.com/); [corpus page](https://debate-erc.com/corpus/); [CORDIS project record](https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/771589).

paper_heading: University of Würzburg, *Arabic and Latin Corpus*
summary_text: The University of Würzburg’s *Arabic and Latin Corpus* catalogs and digitizes Arabic–Latin translations from roughly the tenth through the fourteenth centuries, providing citable digital materials concerning texts, authors, translators, and witnesses. Its primary achievement is transmission infrastructure: it supports access, comparison, and historical study of cross-language movement rather than automatic reasoning about whether an Arabic argument and its Latin translation preserve the same premises, modality, quantification, or warrant. For scholastic computational work, the corpus is especially important because Arabic–Latin translation networks shaped the availability and vocabulary of medieval philosophy and science, yet bilingual alignment alone does not establish inferential equivalence. The resource therefore belongs in the prerequisite corpus layer, with argument-level translation evaluation remaining an open research problem. Verified records: [University of Würzburg project page](https://www.uni-wuerzburg.de/en/zpd/projects/); [Arabic and Latin Corpus site](https://www.arabic-latin-corpus.philosophie.uni-wuerzburg.de/).

paper_heading: UniQ: database of the Prague debate on universals
summary_text: UniQ is a specialized database developed by the Institute of Philosophy of the Czech Academy of Sciences for the medieval debate on universals at the University of Prague between 1348 and 1500. It interlinks philosophical texts, authors, manuscripts, bibliographic sources, dating, authorship information, digital editions, and manuscript witnesses, and provides separate tools for manuscript and text records using linked-data principles. This is a debate-centered corpus and bibliographic graph, not AI reasoning: its relations describe scholarly and transmission entities rather than extracted premises, objections, replies, or formal validity judgments. UniQ is nevertheless a strong model for provenance-aware organization of a specific scholastic controversy and could serve as an upstream layer for argument annotation or model evaluation. Verified record: [Digital Humanities project page](https://digitalhumanities.cz/en/db/uniq-2/).

paper_heading: Dutilh Novaes, *Formalizing Medieval Logical Theories: Suppositio, Consequentiae and Obligationes* (2007)
summary_text: Dutilh Novaes develops historically informed formal reconstructions of medieval theories of supposition, consequence, and obligationes, presenting supposition theory as algorithmic hermeneutics, analyzing consequence with tools related to model theory and two-dimensional semantics, and treating obligationes as logical games. Unlike the other retained items, this book directly addresses formal representations of historical reasoning, but it is a philosophical and interpretive formalization rather than a trained AI system or corpus-scale argument miner. Its central methodological value is its warning that formalization is not neutral transcription: the choice of representation must preserve the conceptual and logical practices of the historical tradition instead of silently replacing them with modern predicate logic. The book supplies the strongest retained precedent for actual reasoning-oriented modeling, while leaving open the alignment of formal structures with manuscript passages, textual variants, competing interpretations, and executable evaluation over large scholastic corpora. Verified record: [Springer book page](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4020-5853-0).

paper_heading: Betti and van den Berg (eds.), *Data-Driven History of Ideas* and the e-Ideas program
summary_text:
The data-driven history-of-ideas program represented by Betti and van den Berg combines qualitative scholarship with quantitative and computational methods for tracing the origins, development, and spread of concepts, while emphasizing the need to represent concepts rather than merely count words and to build high-quality multilingual corpora. The related e-Ideas project combines ontology design, NLP-based machine learning, and distributional semantics under the principle that domain expertise must guide bottom-up corpus exploration. This is computational intellectual history and concept analysis, not direct argument reasoning over scholastic quaestiones: concept trajectories, topic distributions, and semantic proximity can reveal patterns but do not by themselves identify the argumentative function of a term inside an objection, authority citation, or *respondeo*. The methodological precedent is valuable for corpus-scale conceptual comparison, but transfer to medieval scholastic texts would require genre-aware segmentation, historical validation, and explicit separation of concept modeling from inference checking. Verified records: [Data-Driven History of Ideas collection](https://openhumanitiesdata.metajnl.com/collections/historyofideas); [e-Ideas project](https://conceptsinmotion.org/e-ideas/).

## Overall finding

Across the fifteen retained sources, the dominant contribution is infrastructure: digitized or searchable corpora, HTR, linguistic annotation, dependency parsing, linked data, authorship/transmission analysis, and debate or manuscript metadata. These systems are essential prerequisites for scholastic AI but should not be described as reasoning systems merely because they use transformers, machine learning, knowledge graphs, or statistical text analysis. Dutilh Novaes provides the clearest retained precedent for formalized historical reasoning, while Maliszewski provides the closest direct computational study of scholastic reportationes; neither supplies an evaluated end-to-end system that takes a medieval quaestio or disputation as input and produces a provenance-preserving, historically validated argument graph with checked inference. The defensible open space is therefore the missing middle between corpus infrastructure and formal reasoning: genre-aware argument-role annotation, explicit provenance and uncertainty, alignment between source passages and alternative formalizations, and evaluation that separates textual fidelity, historical adequacy, argument-form recognition, and logical validity.

paper_heading: Uckelman (2013), “Medieval Disputationes de obligationibus as Formal Dialogue Systems”
summary_text: Structure: The paper treats a medieval *obligatio* as an alternating dialogue between an Opponent and a Respondent, beginning from a positum and governed by rules for admitting, denying, or responding to propositions. Method: Uckelman reconstructs one medieval obligation theory in Prakken’s formal dialogue-system framework and gives it a Dynamic Epistemic Logic semantics, including dialogue states and conditions for consistency or successful response. Finding: The analysis shows that medieval obligational disputation can be represented as an executable formal dialogue system rather than merely described historically. Limitation: The implementation covers a particular family of obligationes, leaves some proof-system and knowledge assumptions under-specified, and identifies complexity questions for future work; it is not a full Thomistic *quaestio*. Scholastic overlap: This is the closest protocol-level analogue in the set because it directly models regulated opposition, constrained reply, and terminal evaluation, although it lacks the named *sed contra*, *respondeo*, and reply-to-objection stages. Source: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10503-012-9266-7

paper_heading: Maudet, Parsons & Rahwan (2007), “Argumentation in Multi-Agent Systems: Context and Recent Developments”
summary_text: Structure: This survey organizes computational argumentation around conflicting arguments, their interaction, and dialogue protocols across reasoning and communication tasks. Method: It reviews argumentation-based belief revision, deliberation, planning, persuasion, inquiry, negotiation, and dialogue games, including locutions and commencement, commitment, combination, and termination rules. Finding: The survey argues that argumentation supplies a principled way for agents to reconcile information and reach consistent conclusions, while argument schemes and critical questions provide structured ways to challenge claims. Limitation: It is a selective, explicitly “idiosyncratic” survey rather than a single implemented system, and its general dialogue-game treatment does not prescribe a scholastic answer schema. Scholastic overlap: Its rule-governed proponent/opponent interaction and critical-question machinery map naturally onto objection generation and reply control, while its warning against overly rigid proof dialogues supports flexible handling of alternative scholastic replies. Source: https://web.mit.edu/irahwan/www/docs/argmas2006survey.pdf

paper_heading: Castagna, Kökciyan, Sassoon, Parsons & Sklar (2024), “Computational Argumentation-based Chatbots: a Survey”
summary_text: Structure: The paper classifies argumentation-based chatbots by four functions—argument extraction, reply structuring, argumentation-based reasoning, and reply delivery—and surveys dialogue types such as inquiry, persuasion, deliberation, negotiation, verification, and education. Method: The authors define computational-argumentation chatbot criteria, review systems against abstract and structured argumentation frameworks, argument schemes, critical questions, semantics, and evaluation practices, then synthesize benefits and open problems for generative-LLM chatbots. Finding: Computational argumentation offers a route to more coherent, inspectable, and explainable chatbot responses, but the literature contains relatively few mature systems and evaluations are uneven. Limitation: The survey depends on heterogeneous prior systems, many of which are domain-limited, knowledge-base dependent, or unable to support broad conversational interaction; it does not itself implement or validate a complete disputation engine. Scholastic overlap: Its argument graphs, typed attacks, critical questions, and protocol-based reply structures provide a broad substrate for a machine-readable objection-to-reply pipeline, but the scholastic stages and distinction between objection types remain to be specified. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2401.03454v1

paper_heading: Bolton, Calderwood, Christensen, Kafrouni & Drori (2020), “High Quality Real-Time Structured Debate Generation”
summary_text: Structure: The system represents a debate as a tree of arguments and debate paths, with stance-based branching and a high-level grammar for multi-turn generation. Method: The authors train and evaluate a framework over a corpus of tree-structured debates annotated with argument metadata; generation is designed to be embedding-model agnostic and is assessed using competitive-debate criteria for style, content, and strategy. Finding: The system produces complex debates in real time at quality judged close to human performance on those metrics, and releases data, models, and code for reproducibility. Limitation: The evaluation does not test whether a debate is complete or covers the most important points, and generated responses can contain unknown-token artifacts that may bias human judgments; the structure is stance-oriented rather than semantically typed. Scholastic overlap: Debate trees and paths are a strong structural analogue for a root question with nested objections and replies, but the system lacks explicit *sed contra*, *respondeo*, role semantics, and per-objection resolution. Source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.00209

paper_heading: Kargupta, Agarwal, August & Han (2025), “Tree-of-Debate: Multi-Persona Debate Trees Elicit Critical Thinking for Scientific Comparative Analysis”
summary_text: Structure: Tree-of-Debate turns papers into specialized LLM personas and expands a dynamically branching debate tree whose nodes compare contributions, similarities, and differences before synthesis. Method: The authors combine segment-level retrieval, persona construction, self-deliberation, adaptive debate-depth expansion, and debate synthesis, then compare against baselines on scientific comparative-analysis datasets using domain-expert and human evaluations. Finding: Structured debate substantially improves contextualization—reported at an average 95.21% versus 75.57% for the strongest baseline—and supports richer comparative summaries, though gains vary by domain and depth. Limitation: Factuality can decline in domains with less representation in model pretraining, and the approach remains dependent on LLM retrieval, persona quality, and debate-depth choices; its target is literature comparison rather than proposition-level truth adjudication. Scholastic overlap: Specialized disputant roles and dynamic branching resemble assigned participants and expanding objection/counter-objection trees, but the system does not impose a canonical *quaestio* protocol or a principled *respondeo*. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1422/ ; https://arxiv.org/html/2502.14767v2

paper_heading: Vasileiou, Kumar, Yeoh, Son & Toni (2024), “Dialectical Reconciliation via Structured Argumentative Dialogues”
summary_text: Structure: DR-Arg models an explainer agent and an explainee whose knowledge differs, using structured arguments and counterarguments in a dialogue that terminates when the explainee understands the relevant decision model. Method: The paper gives operational semantics and theoretical guarantees for termination and success, then evaluates the framework through computational experiments and human-subject studies. Finding: Argumentative dialogue is presented as a viable way to reconcile knowledge discrepancies and improve human understanding of AI decisions, extending model-reconciliation approaches beyond single-shot explanations and assumed human models. Limitation: The framework is aimed at explainability and convergence on an AI decision, not at open-ended truth-seeking or historical scholastic disputation; its understanding metric and domain assumptions constrain generalization. Scholastic overlap: It is close to an explanatory *respondeo*: the explainer gives reasons, addresses counterarguments, and seeks a satisfactory reconciliation, but it does not explicitly separate objections, *sed contra*, main determination, and individual replies. Source: https://proceedings.kr.org/2024/73/kr2024-0073-vasileiou-et-al.pdf

paper_heading: Faugier, Armetta, Bonifati & Yun (2024), “Assisted Debate Builder with Large Language Models”
summary_text: Structure: ADBL2 represents debates as bipolar argumentation trees whose edges encode support or attack, while preserving an editable, inspectable tree artifact. Method: The authors build an open-source debate-builder interface, use relation-based argument mining to verify existing relations and propose new arguments, and fine-tune a Mistral-7B model for relation classification across domains. Finding: The reported fine-tuned model reaches 90.59% overall F1 and is described as outperforming prior approaches, making it useful for semi-automated construction and correction of debate graphs. Limitation: The paper is a demonstration and relation-mining system rather than a complete dialogue manager; support/attack labels do not by themselves capture distinctions such as undercutting, qualification, distinction, or reply-to-reply, and performance depends on the available datasets and domains. Scholastic overlap: ADBL2 supplies the graph-construction layer needed to turn textual objections and replies into linked, reviewable structures, but it does not decide the scholastic role or discharge status of a move. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.13015

paper_heading: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum & Mordatch (2023), “Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate”
summary_text: Structure: Multiple instances of a language model independently propose answers and reasoning, debate them over several rounds, and converge on a common final answer. Method: The authors apply a shared debate procedure and prompts to black-box models across mathematical, strategic, and factuality-oriented tasks, comparing multiagent debate with single-model baselines. Finding: The paper reports improved mathematical and strategic reasoning and better factual validity, including fewer fallacious answers and hallucinations. Limitation: The protocol is primarily prompt-defined, and the work does not provide explicit argument types, provenance links, formal attack semantics, or a proof that the final consensus correctly resolves every objection; “debate” can therefore function as persuasive aggregation rather than inspectable disputation. Scholastic overlap: Its rounds of opposition followed by synthesis resemble objection, response, and judgment procedurally, but it lacks a stable question-centered schema and a reasoned distinction between main answer and replies. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325

paper_heading: Khan et al. (2024), “Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers”
summary_text: Structure: Two stronger LLM debaters argue for opposing answers while a weaker model or human judge selects between them. Method: The study evaluates debate as a way for non-experts to assess expert-level answers and additionally optimizes debaters for persuasiveness without direct ground-truth labels. Finding: Debate improves answer selection, with the abstract reporting 76% accuracy for non-expert models and 88% for humans versus naive baselines of 48% and 60%; unsupervised persuasion optimization further improves truth identification. Limitation: The setup fixes two opposing sides and delegates resolution to a judge, so it does not require the Respondent to integrate objections into a principled determination; performance also depends on judge competence and persuasive asymmetries. Scholastic overlap: The paper operationalizes adversarial objection as a truth-seeking aid before judgment, but its winner-selection format is only a procedural near-analogue to disputation and lacks formal replies, distinctions, and authority handling. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06782

paper_heading: Hadoux & Hunter (2017), “Strategic Sequences of Arguments for Persuasion Using Decision Trees”
summary_text: Structure: A persuasion dialogue is represented as a decision tree containing possible moves, chance or uncertainty, belief updates, and terminal valuations. Method: The authors transform persuasion into a decision problem, define update and valuation functions, compare established decision rules for selecting argument sequences, and analyze their behavior under uncertainty about the persuadee’s model. Finding: The framework shows how decision rules can prioritize moves strategically; in the reported experiments, MaxiMax performs best when the persuadee model is accurate, while rule performance changes as model error grows. Limitation: The objective is persuasive utility rather than correctness or principled discharge of objections, and practical use requires a suitable valuation function, update function, and model of the interlocutor. Scholastic overlap: It offers a planning mechanism for choosing which objection, critical question, or reply to present next, but its optimization target must be replaced or constrained by scholastic relevance and argumentative validity. Source: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/10673/10532

paper_heading: Gorur, Rago & Toni (2024), “Can Large Language Models perform Relation-based Argument Mining?”
summary_text: Structure: The paper treats relation-based argument mining as classification of relations among argument components, principally support and attack, as a prerequisite for building argument structures. Method: It evaluates prompted general-purpose and quantized open-source LLMs on ten datasets and compares them with a RoBERTa baseline. Finding: The study reports that Llama 70B-4bit and Mixtral 8x7B-4bit surpass the RoBERTa baseline, with Llama 70B-4bit performing better at the cost of slower inference and greater GPU requirements. Limitation: The main experiments use a binary support/attack task even though practical applications often require a ternary no-relation label; datasets are English-only, models are constrained by hardware, and the method uses prompting rather than fine-tuning. Scholastic overlap: This is enabling infrastructure for a disputation parser because a system must identify whether a passage supports, attacks, or relates to another, but the coarse relation inventory does not yet distinguish objection, rebuttal, undercutter, qualification, or reply. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2402.11243

paper_heading: Peldszus & Stede (2019), “Determining Relative Argument Specificity and Stance for Complex Argumentative Structures”
summary_text: Structure: The paper studies manually curated argument trees for 741 controversial topics, with 95,312 claims and generally two-to-six levels of depth, focusing on stance and relative specificity within complex structures. Method: It compares feature-based logistic regression, bag-of-words models, and fine-tuned BERT under controls for path distance, parent-child relation, and stance similarity. Finding: Claim length is strongly predictive of specificity; fine-tuned BERT performs best overall, while stance is easier for parent-child pairs and specificity becomes harder when claims are linguistically similar or evaluated under tighter controls. Limitation: The dataset and task address classification rather than dialogue generation or reply validation, and the authors leave integration into coherent argument generation for future work. Scholastic overlap: Specificity and stance modeling can help a scholastic system determine whether an objection targets the whole conclusion, a particular premise, or a narrower inference, supporting typed replies and distinctions rather than flat pro/con labeling. Source: https://aclanthology.org/P19-1456.pdf

paper_heading: Hodges, “Ibn Sīnā on Analysis: 1. Proof Search. Or: Abstract State Machines as a Tool for History of Logic”
summary_text: Hodges studies Avicenna’s discussion of analysis in *Qiyās* as a historical proof-search procedure for syllogisms, representing its states and transitions with an Abstract State Machine. The evidence is a close reading, translation, and formal reconstruction of the Arabic logical passage rather than a machine-learning experiment or benchmark. Its main limitation is scope: it formalizes one logical procedure and does not model the semantics, rhetoric, or social context of broader kalām or scholastic debate. For this project, it is the strongest direct precedent for converting a medieval Arabic reasoning procedure into an executable, inspectable computational representation, especially a target representation for premises, transformations, and conclusions. [1]

paper_heading: Hodges, “A Correctness Proof for al-Barakāt’s Logical Diagrams”
summary_text: This article reconstructs Abū al-Barakāt’s twelfth-century diagrammatic method for finding conclusions of premise-pairs and identifying pairs with no conclusion, then gives a rigorous proof that the procedure is correct. The computational method is symbolic reconstruction and correctness proof, not NLP: the author reverse-engineers a procedure that the medieval source presents without instructions or proof. The evidence is the logical behavior of the reconstructed diagrams and the proof that the resulting outputs match the intended syllogistic consequences. The limitation is that the system remains a narrow formal treatment of syllogistic inference and does not address historical language processing, argument identification, or theological disagreement. It matters here as a model for translating Arabic logical artifacts into verifiable symbolic-AI components rather than treating them as opaque historical prose. [2]

paper_heading: Abdelwahab, Daghbouche, and Shannan, “The Algorithm of Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh) with Validation of an Entscheidungsproblem”
summary_text: This paper proposes a formal account of *uṣūl al-fiqh* by expressing selected jurisprudential questions through mathematical logic, a logic-query language, and a generic algorithm intended to decide legal rulings. Its method is conceptual formalization using subsets of first-order logic, with discussion of completeness, decidability, complexity, and an Islamic-law Entscheidungsproblem. The evidence is the paper’s definitions, worked methodological distinctions, and proposed formal architecture, not a released implementation, corpus, or empirical evaluation. Its limitation is substantial: broad claims about complete algorithmic coverage and decidability are programmatic and should not be treated as validated performance results; it also concerns jurisprudence rather than kalām proper. It is relevant as an adjacent example of rule-based knowledge representation for Islamic scholastic reasoning and as a caution against confusing formal specification with demonstrated historical or legal competence. [3]

paper_heading: Abdelwahab et al., “Computational Extraction of Legal Causes via al-Ṣabr wa al-Taqsīm: A Set-Theoretic Formalization for Closed Fiqh Chapters”
summary_text: This paper formalizes the classical uṣūl al-fiqh technique of *al-ṣabr wa al-taqsīm*—examination and division—as a set-theoretic procedure for extracting candidate legal causes within closed jurisprudential chapters. The computational method maps the traditional elimination and classification process into sets, predicates, and operations that can in principle support rule-based extraction. The evidence is the explicit mathematical reconstruction of the method and its application to legal-cause analysis, rather than a trained NLP model or benchmarked information-extraction system. Its limitation is the closed-domain and highly formal setting: results do not establish robustness on varied Arabic legal prose, contested interpretations, or theological argument. For this project, it demonstrates how a historically situated scholastic technique can become an executable intermediate layer between textual evidence and an argument graph, while confirming that current formalization work is concentrated in fiqh rather than comparative kalām. [4]

paper_heading: Maliszewski, “It Takes a Village to Write a Book: Mapping Anonymous Contributions in Stephen Langton’s *Quaestiones Theologiae*”
summary_text: Maliszewski presents a registered-report protocol for analyzing collaborative production and editorial layers in Stephen Langton’s medieval Christian theological *quaestiones*, which derive from *reportationes* of oral teaching. The method combines handwritten-text recognition, automated transcription alignment, stylometry based on frequent words, part-of-speech sequences, pseudo-affixes, and unsupervised clustering. The evidence includes exploratory principal-component analyses separating Langton’s corpus from other scholastic collections and revealing internal stylistic diversity, while the proposed study compares manually edited with HTR-extracted data. Its chief limitation is that short *quaestiones* provide weak stylometric samples and the work primarily identifies authorship and transmission layers, not argumentative structure or doctrinal validity. It is directly useful here as a Christian scholastic preprocessing and corpus-method precedent: reliable modeling of disputation requires first separating reportators, editors, witnesses, and textual layers. [5][6]

paper_heading: Maliszewski, published Cambridge version of “It Takes a Village to Write a Book”
summary_text: The Cambridge-published version confirms the same registered-report study and supplies the bibliographic and publication record for the Langton investigation: the corpus contains multiple versions of many *quaestiones*, and the proposed workflow compares stylometry on manually edited text with transformer-based HTR output. Its computational method remains function-word and other stylometric features, POS sequences, pseudo-affixes, clustering, and transcription alignment, while the evidence is the article’s exploratory PCA and corpus statistics rather than a completed argument-mining evaluation. The limitation is unchanged: short texts weaken authorial-style inference, and authorship or editorial-layer detection does not recover the semantic structure of scholastic objections and replies. The published record is relevant to this project as a verified, reusable computational-humanities protocol for corpus formation and transmission-aware preprocessing; it should be treated as the same study as the open preprint, not as independent corroboration. [6]

paper_heading: Lange et al., “Text Mining Islamic Law”
summary_text: This article surveys and demonstrates the use of digital-humanities and text-mining methods in Islamic legal studies, including corpus construction, computational comparison, and analysis of Qur’anic and legal materials across schools of law. Its method is empirical text mining combined with historical and legal interpretation, using machine-readable corpora to test or refine claims in the secondary literature. The evidence is the article’s comparative computational analyses, which in some cases confirm scholarly claims and in others correct them. Its limitation is disciplinary and representational: text mining can reveal distributional and textual patterns, but it does not by itself recover the full force of legal reasoning, authority, intent, or dialectical exchange. The relation to this project is infrastructural and methodological: it shows that computational Islamic studies can be historically meaningful when corpus design and domain interpretation remain explicit, while underscoring the lack of mature argument-mining resources for kalām. [7]

paper_heading: OpenITI, Open Islamicate Texts Initiative
summary_text: OpenITI is a machine-actionable corpus initiative for premodern Arabic and other Islamicate texts rather than a single research paper or AI model. Its computational contribution is corpus encoding, normalization, metadata, versioning, and machine-readable text organization designed to support search, quantitative analysis, authorship study, terminology extraction, and future NLP. The evidence is the initiative’s description of its corpus goals, scholarly data model, and coverage of the written Arabic and Islamicate heritage. Its limitations include uneven edition alignment, OCR and transcription noise, incomplete genre and author metadata, and the need for expert validation before using texts as gold-standard training data. For this project, OpenITI is the principal enabling infrastructure for assembling comparable corpora across kalām, falsafa, fiqh, Jewish-Arabic philosophy, and related traditions; it is a prerequisite resource, not evidence that comparative scholastic argument mining has already been solved. [8]

paper_heading: Yousef et al., “Enhancing State-of-the-Art NLP Models for Classical Arabic”
summary_text: Yousef and colleagues develop Classical-Arabic NLP resources and fine-tune deep-learning models for named-entity recognition, person-relationship classification, toponym classification, onomastic-section detection, onomastic-element classification, and date recognition. The method uses a large OpenITI-derived subcorpus, active learning, expert annotation, iterative correction, and fine-tuning of Classical-Arabic transformer models. The evidence includes reported improvements such as fine-tuned NER F1 scores around 94% for persons and toponyms and an onomastic-boundary F1 around 88%, alongside a corpus of roughly 71 million tokens and hundreds of thousands of biographies. Limitations include the in-progress status, task-specific biography domain, sparse expert labels, weaker performance for underrepresented classes and toponym relations, and no direct modeling of premises or rebuttals. It supplies the language-processing layer needed before extracting authorities, participants, and textual relations from historical Islamic scholastic works. [9]

paper_heading: Hawwari, Diab, and Zaghouani, “A Pilot PropBank Annotation for Quranic Arabic”
summary_text: This paper creates a pilot Quranic Arabic PropBank by assigning predicate-argument structures and semantic roles to the 50 most frequent verbs in the Quranic Arabic Dependency Treebank. The computational method combines dependency syntax, manually created verb frames, Arabic root-meaning references, double annotation, and adjudication; the pilot covers 7,227 verbal occurrences and is intended eventually to extend to all 1,466 Quranic verb types. The evidence is the feasibility of constructing frame files and the observed sense differences between Quranic Arabic and modern newswire Arabic, including greater ambiguity in the Quranic resource. Its limitation is coverage: the pilot annotates only 50 verbs and semantic roles are not equivalent to discourse-level argumentation, doctrinal inference, or intertextual authority. For this project, it is a foundational semantic layer for distinguishing linguistic predicate structure from later theological interpretation and for building Arabic resources that can feed argument-mining pipelines. [10]

paper_heading: Altammami and Atwell, “Challenging the Transformer-based Models with a Classical Arabic Dataset: Quran and Hadith”
summary_text: This study evaluates monolingual, bilingual, and multilingual transformer models on semantic relatedness between Quran verses and Hadith teachings, using a deliberately difficult Classical-Arabic dataset assembled with expert consultation. The method trains or fine-tunes models on Quran–Quran relatedness data and tests generalization on Quran–Hadith pairs, reducing the risk that random splits merely measure memorization. The evidence is the dataset-construction methodology, cross-domain evaluation, and the reported finding that current models struggle with the complex semantics, orthography, rhetoric, and implicit meanings of Quranic and Hadith texts. Its limitation is task scope: binary semantic relatedness is not structured argument mining, and performance depends on expert pair construction rather than a complete model of religious reasoning. It provides a useful evaluation warning for this project: strong results on modern Arabic or in-domain splits do not establish competence with historically situated scholastic language or reasoning. [11]

paper_heading: Alnefaie, Atwell, and Alsalka, “HAQA and QUQA: Constructing Two Arabic Question-Answering Corpora for the Quran and Hadith”
summary_text: This paper constructs two reusable Arabic QA corpora: HAQA for Hadith and QUQA for Quran questions, containing 1,598 and 3,382 question–answer pairs respectively. The method integrates existing datasets with expert-authored books, OCR, manual review, automated cleaning, metadata construction, and source/evidence fields distinguishing expert commentary from answer-bearing Quranic or Hadith passages. The evidence is the released corpus design, source-selection process, explicit credibility metadata, and stated coverage and size. Its limitations are that QA pairs are not annotated for argumentative roles, legal-school disagreement, or dialectical relations, and the mixture of source text and expert explanation can complicate faithfulness evaluation. It is relevant as a nearby benchmark and retrieval resource for Islamic textual systems, especially for testing citation grounding and answer extraction before attempting historically faithful modeling of kalām debates. [12]

paper_heading: “Computational Linguistic Analysis of the Biblical Text”
summary_text: This book chapter surveys computational-linguistic approaches to biblical languages and textual analysis, including corpus methods, linguistic theories, databases, and computational representations of Biblical Hebrew and related scriptural languages. Its method is synthetic and methodological rather than a single new model: it compares how different linguistic frameworks shape computational analysis of the Biblical text. The evidence is the chapter’s discussion of existing computational resources, theories, and applications across biblical-language scholarship. Its limitation is that it provides enabling infrastructure and methodological orientation, not an annotated corpus or system for medieval Jewish scholastic argument, Christian *quaestiones*, or comparative theological debate. For this project, it supplies the comparative-tradition bridge: Hebrew and biblical NLP can support historical textual normalization and semantic analysis, but those capabilities must not be mistaken for computational modeling of Jewish scholastic reasoning. [13]

paper_heading: Tsarfaty et al., “What’s Wrong with Hebrew NLP? And How to Make it Right”
summary_text: This paper presents ONLP/YAP, a joint morpho-syntactic parsing framework for Modern Hebrew designed to avoid error propagation in morphologically ambiguous Semitic text. The computational method jointly searches over morphological segmentation, disambiguation, part-of-speech and feature assignment, lemmas, and dependency trees using structured prediction and beam search rather than a brittle pipeline. The evidence is the system architecture, open implementation and output layers, and reported improvements over competing Hebrew models, with support for lattices and out-of-domain analysis. Its limitation is domain and task mismatch: it targets Modern Hebrew language processing and does not analyze medieval Jewish philosophy, rabbinic disputation, or arguments; performance also depends on lexicon coverage and annotated data. It is relevant as transferable infrastructure for Jewish scholastic corpora, where historically sensitive segmentation and syntactic analysis are prerequisites for reliable semantic and argument-level extraction. [14]

paper_heading: Mirarab and DarestaniFarahani, “Explainable Large Language Model for Islamic and Humanities Sciences Based on Knowledge Graphs”
summary_text: This article proposes a conceptual framework integrating knowledge graphs with large language models for Islamic studies and the humanities, emphasizing explainability, conceptual inference, and representation of complex relations. The method is an analytical study based on a systematic literature review and purposeful selection of existing knowledge-graph and LLM resources; its stated output is a framework rather than a trained system. The evidence is the article’s explicit architecture, metadata, and claims that graph representations can organize concepts while LLMs extract and process natural-language information. Its central limitation is evidentiary: no publicly reported benchmark, corpus, ablation, expert agreement study, or historical kalām evaluation demonstrates that the proposed framework works in practice. It is nevertheless directly relevant as a design hypothesis for an ontology of doctrines, authorities, objections, distinctions, and inferential relations, provided the project treats it as a proposal rather than validated evidence. [15]

paper_heading: Mouhoub, “Islamic Large Language Models: From Knowledge Acquisition to Trustworthy and Hallucination-Resistant AI”
summary_text: Mouhoub surveys Islamic LLMs and trustworthy Islamic AI across Arabic NLP, Islamic corpora, Quranic QA, knowledge benchmarks, retrieval-augmented generation, legal reasoning, inheritance reasoning, hallucination evaluation, and citation-aware generation. The method is a structured literature survey and research agenda organized around source hierarchy, exact citation verification, Classical-Arabic variation, madhhab-aware disagreement, retrieval, and expert evaluation. The evidence is the synthesis of existing models, resources, and benchmarks, together with the argument that fluency is insufficient without grounded sources and verifiable reasoning. Its limitation is that it is a survey rather than a new empirical benchmark or system, and its broad field map may include emerging resources whose comparative validity remains unsettled. For this project, it provides the clearest current specification of evaluation requirements: source-grounded extraction, explicit uncertainty and disagreement, citation accuracy, and tests against fabricated authorities and anachronistic reasoning. [16]

paper_heading: Lawrence and Reed, “Argument Mining: A Survey”
summary_text: Lawrence and Reed define argument mining as the automatic identification and extraction of inferential structure expressed in natural language and review methods for detecting argumentative components and relations. The computational method surveyed includes discourse analysis, machine learning, structured prediction, component classification, relation identification, and increasingly deeper modeling of reasoning structure. The evidence is a broad synthesis of argument-mining tasks, datasets, techniques, and unresolved challenges across domains rather than a domain-specific Islamic or scholastic experiment. Its limitation is transfer: generic argument-mining categories and benchmarks do not automatically capture scholastic distinctions, authority relations, objections, replies, modality, genre conventions, or multilingual historical variation. It is the methodological anchor for this project because it defines the target capability, but it must be combined with expert-annotated corpora and historically grounded schemas for kalām, Jewish philosophy, and Christian *quaestiones*. [17]

paper_heading: Verification and project-level finding
summary_text:
The 17 retained items were checked against the supplied URLs and accessible publisher, repository, ACL, arXiv, Cambridge, Brill, OpenITI, and author-page records; the Hodges proof-search paper was additionally cross-checked against an accessible mirror because the retained author PDF did not download in the local manifest, and the chapter/PDF records with OCR restrictions were verified through bibliographic or publisher metadata. The set contains four symbolic/formalization studies, one computational Christian-scholastic protocol, Islamic-law text-mining and corpus infrastructure, Classical-Arabic and Hebrew NLP resources, Quran/Hadith QA and semantic datasets, one Islamic knowledge-graph/LLM proposal, a current Islamic-LLM survey, and a general argument-mining survey. Collectively, the evidence supports a sparse-and-fragmented literature finding: the strongest computational precedents formalize procedures or build enabling corpora, while no retained source provides a mature, openly benchmarked, multilingual AI system for historically faithful comparative modeling of kalām, Jewish scholastic argument, and Christian scholastic *quaestiones*.
